<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
The \emph{mixing time} of a Lindbladian $\mathcal{L}$ with a well-defined infinite-time limit $P_\mathcal{L}$ for $\varepsilon>0$ is
\begin{align*}
    \tau_{\operatorname{mix}}^{\mathcal{L}}(\varepsilon):=\inf\Bigl\{t>0:\sup_{\rho\in\mathcal{D}_1(\mathcal{H})} \|e^{t\mathcal{L}}(\rho)-P_\mathcal{L}(\rho)\|_1<\varepsilon\Bigr\}.
\end{align*}
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- definition-2: body_md -->
For a family $(\mathcal{L}_N)_N$ with well-defined infinite-time limits, we say that the family is \emph{rapidly mixing} if there are constants $a,q>0$, independent of $N$, such that
\begin{align}
    \label{eq:rapid-mixing-time} \tau_{\operatorname{mix}}^{\mathcal{L}_N}\leq a\left[\log(eN)\right]^q.
\end{align}
<!-- end definition-2 -->
<!-- definition-3: body_md -->
For a family $(\mathcal{L}_N)_N$ with well-defined infinite-time limits, we say that the family is \emph{rapidly mixing with constant decay rate} if there are constants $\gamma>0$ and $c\geq0$, independent of $N$, and a prefactor $C_N\geq1$ satisfying $C_N=O(N^c)$ such that
\begin{align}
    \label{eq:sufficient} \sup_{\rho\in\mathcal{D}_1(\mathcal{H})}\|e^{t\mathcal{L}_N}(\rho)-P_{\mathcal{L}_N}(\rho)\|_1\leq C_N e^{-\gamma t},\qquad t\geq0.
\end{align}
<!-- end definition-3 -->
<!-- definition-4: body_md -->
For a family $(\mathcal{L}_N)_N$ of Lindbladians, we say that the family is \emph{uniformly rapidly mixing} if there exist constants $a,q,R_0>0$ such that, for every lattice $\Lambda$ in the family, every $x\in\Lambda$, and every $R\geq R_0$, the restriction to $A=b_x(R)$ has a well-defined infinite-time limit and
\begin{align}
    \tau_{\operatorname{mix}}^{\mathcal{L}_A}\leq a\left[\log(e|A|)\right]^q,
\end{align}
where the constants are independent of $\Lambda,x$, and $R$. We say that the family is \emph{uniformly rapidly mixing with constant decay rate} if there are constants $C,\gamma>0$ and $p\geq0$, uniform in the same parameters, such that
\begin{align}
    \label{eq:uniform-rapid-mixing} \sup_{\rho\in\mathcal{D}_1(\mathcal{H}_A)}\|e^{t\mathcal{L}_A}(\rho)-P_{\mathcal{L}_A}(\rho)\|_1\le C|A|^p e^{-\gamma t},\qquad t\geq0,
\end{align}
<!-- end definition-4 -->
<!-- definition-5: body_md -->
Let $\sigma\succ0$ be a stationary state of $\mathcal{L}$. We say that $\mathcal{L}$ satisfies a \emph{modified logarithmic Sobolev inequality} (MLSI) with constant $\alpha>0$ if, for every density matrix $\rho\in\mathcal{D}_1(\mathcal{H})$,
\begin{align}
    \label{eq:MLSI} 2\alpha\,D(\rho\|\sigma)\le \operatorname{EP}_\mathcal{L}(\rho).
\end{align}
Here $\operatorname{EP}_\mathcal{L}$, called the entropy production, is given by
\begin{align}
    \operatorname{EP}_\mathcal{L}(\rho):=-\operatorname{Tr}[\mathcal{L}(\rho)(\log\rho-\log\sigma)].
\end{align}
The optimal constant is denoted by $\alpha(\mathcal{L})$ and is called the modified log-Sobolev constant.
<!-- end definition-5 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:perturbation_fixed_point} 
  \addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{ 
    \texorpdfstring{\protect\cref*{lem:perturbation_fixed_point}}{Result \getrefnumber{lem:perturbation_fixed_point}}: Mixing under a small contractive perturbation} 

Let $\mathcal L_0$ be a Lindbladian with a unique stationary state $\sigma_0$ and a well-defined infinite-time limit. Set $T:=\tau_{\operatorname{mix}}^{\mathcal L_0}(1/2)$, and let $V$ be a Hermiticity-preserving, trace-annihilating linear map.
Define the restricted induced trace norm on traceless Hermitian operators by
\begin{align*}
    \|V\|_{1\to1,0}:=\sup_{\substack{X=X^\dagger,\ \operatorname{Tr} X=0\\X\neq0}}
    \frac{\|V(X)\|_1}{\|X\|_1}.
\end{align*}
For $\varepsilon\geq0$, set $\mathcal L_\varepsilon:=\mathcal L_0+\varepsilon V$ and suppose that $e^{t\mathcal L_\varepsilon}$ is a trace-norm contraction on Hermitian operators for every $t\geq0$. If
\begin{align}
    \varepsilon \|V\|_{1\to1,0}\leq\frac{1}{4T}, \label{eq:generic-perturbation-threshold}
\end{align}
then $\mathcal L_\varepsilon$ has a unique stationary state $\sigma_\varepsilon$ and, for all states $\rho$ and $t\geq0$,
\begin{align}
    \lVert e^{t\mathcal L_\varepsilon}(\rho)-\sigma_\varepsilon\rVert_1
    \leq\frac43e^{-\gamma t}\lVert\rho-\sigma_\varepsilon\rVert_1,
    \qquad \gamma:=\frac{\log(4/3)}{T}. \label{eq:generic-perturbation-bound}
\end{align}
Mixing times $T=O(\operatorname{polylog}N)$ imply rapid mixing; $T=O(1)$ gives constant decay rate.
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:XZeps} 
  \addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{ 
    \texorpdfstring{\protect\cref*{lem:XZeps}}{Result \getrefnumber{lem:XZeps}}: A common full-rank fixed point does not make rapid mixing additive} 

There exist two local, unital, primitive Lindbladian families $(\mathcal{L}_N)_N$ and $(\mathcal{K}_N)_N$ that are both rapidly mixing with constant decay rate and have the same unique fixed point $\sigma_N=2^{-N}\mathbb{I}$, whereas $\mathcal{L}_N+\mathcal{K}_N$ is primitive with fixed point $\sigma_N$ but satisfies
\begin{align}
    \tau_{\operatorname{mix}}^{\mathcal{L}_N+\mathcal{K}_N}=\Omega(N^2).
\end{align}
In particular, the family $(\mathcal{L}_N+\mathcal{K}_N)_N$ is not rapidly mixing.
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- example-1: body_md -->
\label{ex:XZeps}
On a spin chain of $N$ sites, write $\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_N$ and $\mathcal{K}=\mathcal{K}_N$ for the local generators of the families $(\mathcal{L}_N)_N$ and $(\mathcal{K}_N)_N$, with jump operator $Z_j$ at every site $j$ and Hamiltonians $X_j$ and $(\varepsilon_j-1)X_j$, respectively:
\begin{align}
    \mathcal{L}(\rho)=\sum_j\bigl(-i[X_j,\rho]+\mathcal D[Z_j](\rho)\bigr),\qquad \mathcal{K}(\rho)=\sum_j\bigl(-i[(\varepsilon_j-1)X_j,\rho]+\mathcal D[Z_j](\rho)\bigr),
\end{align}
where $\varepsilon_j=1/(j+1)$. Both generators have the unique full-rank fixed point $\sigma=(\mathbb{I}/2)^{\otimes N}$, and both families are rapidly mixing. For every finite $N$, the sum $\mathcal{L}+\mathcal{K}$ is primitive and gapped, but its gap is $\Theta(N^{-2})$ and its mixing time is $\Omega(N^2)$, so $(\mathcal{L}_N+\mathcal{K}_N)_N$ is not rapidly mixing.
<!-- end example-1 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:fermionic-addition} 
  \addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{ 
    \texorpdfstring{\protect\cref*{lem:fermionic-addition}}{Result \getrefnumber{lem:fermionic-addition}}: Translation invariance and fixed local coefficients do not make rapid mixing additive} 

There exist two finite-range, translation-invariant fermionic Lindbladian families $(\mathcal{L}_N^+)_N$ and $(\mathcal{L}_N^-)_N$, indexed by odd $N\geq5$ and with local coefficients independent of $N$, such that both families are uniformly rapidly mixing with constant decay rate and have the same unique full-rank fixed point $\sigma_N=4^{-N}\mathbb{I}$. The sum family $(\mathcal S_N)_N$, with $\mathcal S_N=\mathcal{L}_N^++\mathcal{L}_N^-$, is primitive with the same fixed point at each size, but for every $0<\varepsilon<1$,
\begin{align}
    \tau_{\operatorname{mix}}^{\mathcal S_N}(\varepsilon)
    \geq \frac{N^2}{2\pi^2}\log(\varepsilon^{-1}).
\end{align}
The lower bound persists when the supremum in the mixing time is restricted to parity-even states.
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- example-2: body_md -->
\label{ex:fermionic-addition}
For odd $N\geq5$, let $\Lambda_N=\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$, with two fermionic annihilation operators $a_x,b_x$ in each cell $x$. With indices understood modulo $N$, define
\begin{align}
    H_{\lambda,N}&=\sum_{x\in\Lambda_N}\left[\lambda a_x^\dagger b_x+\frac12(a_{x+1}^\dagger+a_{x-1}^\dagger)b_x+\mathrm{h.c.}\right],\label{eq:fermionic-addition-H-main}\\
    \mathcal{L}_{\lambda,N}(\rho)&=-i[H_{\lambda,N},\rho]+\sum_{x\in\Lambda_N}\left(\mathcal D[a_x](\rho)+\mathcal D[a_x^\dagger](\rho)\right).\label{eq:fermionic-addition-L-main}
\end{align}
Define the families $(\mathcal{L}_N^\pm)_N$ and $(\mathcal S_N)_N$ by $\mathcal{L}_N^\pm=\mathcal{L}_{\pm2,N}$ and $\mathcal S_N=\mathcal{L}_N^++\mathcal{L}_N^-$, and set $\sigma_N=4^{-N}\mathbb{I}$. Then
\begin{align}
    \lVert e^{t\mathcal{L}_N^\pm}-P_{\mathcal{L}_N^\pm}\rVert_\diamond\leq12Ne^{-t/2},\qquad P_{\mathcal{L}_N^\pm}(X)=\operatorname{Tr}(X)\sigma_N.
\end{align}
The same estimate, with $N$ replaced by $|A|$, holds for the restriction to every nonempty set of cells $A$, retaining the on-site jumps and the Hamiltonian terms supported in $A$. The sum $\mathcal S_N=2\mathcal{L}_{0,N}$ is primitive with fixed point $\sigma_N$, but
\begin{align}
    \tau_{\operatorname{mix}}^{\mathcal S_N}(\varepsilon)&\geq\frac{\log(\varepsilon^{-1})}{2r_N}
    \geq\frac{N^2}{2\pi^2}\log(\varepsilon^{-1}),
    &r_N&=1-\sqrt{1-4\sin^2\left(\frac{\pi}{2N}\right)}.
\end{align}
The state establishing this bound has even parity.
<!-- end example-2 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{lem:rm_sum_dissip_only} 
  \addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{ 
    \texorpdfstring{\protect\cref*{lem:rm_sum_dissip_only}}{Result \getrefnumber{lem:rm_sum_dissip_only}}: Dissipation-only rapid mixing is not additive} 

There exist two geometrically local, translation-invariant, zero-Hamiltonian Lindbladian families $(\mathcal{L}_N)_N$ and $(\mathcal{K}_N)_N$ on periodic lattices, each with a unique stationary state and rapid mixing with constant decay rate, such that the stationary states are different and the infinite-time limit of $\mathcal{L}_N+\mathcal{K}_N$ exists, but
\begin{align}
    \tau_{\operatorname{mix}}^{\mathcal{L}_N+\mathcal{K}_N}\geq\frac{N-1}{8}.
\end{align}
The sum family $(\mathcal{L}_N+\mathcal{K}_N)_N$ has a degenerate steady-state subspace at each size.
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- example-3: body_md -->
\label{ex:rows-dissip}\label{ex:rm_sum_dissip_only}
Consider a periodic chain of $N\geq2$ sites, with two qubits $a_i,b_i$ at each site $i$. Define the families $(\mathcal{L}_N)_N$ and $(\mathcal{K}_N)_N$ by writing $\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_N$ and $\mathcal{K}=\mathcal{K}_N$ at each size:
\begin{align}
    \mathcal{L}&=\sum_{i=1}^N\mathcal{D}[L_{a,i}]+\sum_{i=1}^N\mathcal{D}[L_{b,i}]+\sum_{i=1}^N\mathcal{D}[L_{a,b,i}],\notag\\
    \mathcal{K}&=\sum_{i=1}^N\mathcal{D}[K_{a,i}]+\sum_{i=1}^N\mathcal{D}[L_{b,i}]+\sum_{i=1}^N\mathcal{D}[L_{a,b,i}],
\end{align}
with jump operators
\begin{align}
    L_{a,i}&=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\
    0&-1\end{pmatrix}_{a_i},\qquad 1\le i\le N,\notag\\
    K_{a,i}&=\begin{pmatrix}1&-2\\
    0&-1\end{pmatrix}_{a_i},\qquad 1\le i\le N,\notag\\
    L_{b,i}&=\lvert 0\rangle\!\langle 0\rvert_{b_i}\otimes\lvert 0\rangle\!\langle 1\rvert_{b_{i+1}},\qquad 1\le i\le N,\notag\\
    L_{a,b,i}&=\sqrt{\gamma}\,\lvert 1\rangle\!\langle 1\rvert_{a_i}\otimes\lvert 0\rangle\!\langle 1\rvert_{b_i},\qquad 1\le i\le N.
\end{align}
Here $\gamma>0$ is independent of $N$, and the site labels are understood modulo $N$, so $b_{N+1}=b_1$. The bottom jump changes $b_{i+1}$ from $1$ to $0$ when $b_i$ is in state $0$, while the cross jump changes $b_i$ from $1$ to $0$ when $a_i$ is in state $1$. Thus $\mathcal{L}$ and $\mathcal{K}$ are translation invariant and have the same bottom and cross jumps, while the off-diagonal entries of their $a_i$ jumps have opposite signs.

Let $\eta=\begin{pmatrix}\frac56&-\frac13\\-\frac13&\frac16\end{pmatrix}$ be the unique fixed point of the single-qubit dissipator with jump operator $L_a=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$. The Lindbladian $\mathcal{L}$ has the unique fixed point $\sigma_\mathcal{L}=\eta_a^{\otimes N}\otimes\lvert 0^N\rangle\!\langle 0^N\rvert_b$, while $\mathcal{K}$ has the unique fixed point $\sigma_\mathcal{K}=(Z\eta Z)_a^{\otimes N}\otimes\lvert 0^N\rangle\!\langle 0^N\rvert_b$. Both families $(\mathcal{L}_N)_N$ and $(\mathcal{K}_N)_N$ are dissipation-only and rapidly mixing with constant decay rate, but $(\mathcal{L}_N+\mathcal{K}_N)_N$ is not rapidly mixing: for every fixed $0<\delta<1/2$, $\tau_{\operatorname{mix}}^{\mathcal{L}+\mathcal{K}}(\delta)=\Omega(N)$.

Their sum has kernel
\begin{align}
    \ker(\mathcal{L}+\mathcal{K})&=\lvert 0^N\rangle\!\langle 0^N\rvert_a\otimes\mathcal{B}(\mathcal S_b),\qquad \mathcal S_b:=\operatorname{span}\{|0^N\rangle_b,|1^N\rangle_b\},
\end{align}
where $\mathcal{B}(\mathcal S_b)$ is embedded in the $b$-qubit operator algebra and includes coherences between the strings. Its infinite-time limit exists, and the mixing time to this kernel is $\Omega(N)$.
<!-- end example-3 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{lem:rm_sum_hamiltonian} 
  \addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{ 
    \texorpdfstring{\protect\cref*{lem:rm_sum_hamiltonian}}{Result \getrefnumber{lem:rm_sum_hamiltonian}}: A local Hamiltonian can destroy rapid mixing} 

There exist a geometrically local, translation-invariant, zero-Hamiltonian Lindbladian family $(\mathcal{L}_N)_N$ on periodic lattices with a unique stationary state and rapid mixing with constant decay rate, and a translation-invariant on-site Hamiltonian family $(\mathcal{K}_N)_N$ of uniformly bounded local strength, such that the infinite-time limit of $\mathcal{L}_N+\mathcal{K}_N$ exists but
\begin{align}
    \tau_{\operatorname{mix}}^{\mathcal{L}_N+\mathcal{K}_N}\geq\frac{N-1}{4}.
\end{align}
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- example-4: body_md -->
\label{ex:rows-ham} 
  \addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{ 
    \texorpdfstring{\protect\cref*{ex:rows-ham}}{Result \getrefnumber{ex:rows-ham}}: Rapid mixing lost due to the Hamiltonian} 
\label{ex:rm_sum_hamiltonian}
Let $\mathcal{L}$ be the Lindbladian from \cref{ex:rm_sum_dissip_only}. It has the unique fixed point $\sigma_\mathcal{L}=\eta_a^{\otimes N}\otimes\lvert 0^N\rangle\!\langle 0^N\rvert_b$ and satisfies $\tau_{\operatorname{mix}}^\mathcal{L}(\varepsilon)=\mathcal{O}(\log(N/\varepsilon))$. Let $H_i=Y_{a_i}$ and define $(\mathcal{K}_N)_N$ by $\mathcal{K}_N=\mathcal{K}=-i[\sum_{i=1}^NH_i,\cdot]$. Then $(\mathcal{L}_N+\mathcal{K}_N)_N$ is not rapidly mixing: for every fixed $0<\delta<1/2$, $\tau_{\operatorname{mix}}^{\mathcal{L}+\mathcal{K}}(\delta)=\Omega(N)$.
<!-- end example-4 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{lem:sparse-boundary-potential} 
  \addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{ 
    \texorpdfstring{\protect\cref*{lem:sparse-boundary-potential}}{Result \getrefnumber{lem:sparse-boundary-potential}}: An arbitrarily weak local Hamiltonian can destroy rapid mixing} 

There exist a primitive local Lindbladian family, evaluated on chains of $m_N=\Theta(\log N)$ qubits and denoted by $(\mathcal{L}_N)_N$, and, for each $N$, an on-site Hamiltonian generator $\mathcal{K}_N$ of uniformly bounded local strength, such that, for every fixed $\varepsilon>0$, $\mathcal{L}_N+\varepsilon\mathcal{K}_N$ is primitive with the same maximally mixed stationary state as $\mathcal{L}_N$, and
\begin{align}
    \tau_{\operatorname{mix}}^{\mathcal{L}_N}=O((\log N)^{10}),\qquad
    \tau_{\operatorname{mix}}^{\mathcal{L}_N+\varepsilon\mathcal{K}_N}\geq N^{c_\varepsilon+o(1)}
\end{align}
for some $c_\varepsilon>0$. Here $m_N$ is the physical chain length and $N$ is an auxiliary parameter.
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- example-5: body_md -->
\label{ex:sparse-boundary-potential}
Fix $a,J>0$ and set $\gamma=J/2$. For all sufficiently large $N$, let
\begin{align}
    m=m_N:=3\left\lfloor\frac{a\log N}{3}\right\rfloor,
    \qquad \ell:=\frac{m}{3}.
\end{align}
Consider one open chain of $m$ qubits, with sites labelled $1,\ldots,m$, and define
\begin{align}
    H&=-J\sum_{j=1}^{m-1}\bigl(\sigma_j^+\sigma_{j+1}^-+\sigma_j^-\sigma_{j+1}^+\bigr),\label{eq:sparse-H0}\\
    \mathcal{L}_N(\rho)&=-i[H,\rho]+\gamma\sum_{s\in\{1,m\}}\bigl(\mathcal D[\sigma_s^-](\rho)+\mathcal D[\sigma_s^+](\rho)\bigr).\label{eq:sparse-L0}
\end{align}
The dissipation-free interval between the two endpoints has length $m-2=\Theta(\log N)$. Define the on-site potential profile and its Hamiltonian generator by
\begin{align}
    V_N&=\sum_{j=1}^{\ell}n_j+\sum_{j=2\ell+1}^{3\ell}n_j,
    \qquad n_j=\sigma_j^+\sigma_j^-,\label{eq:sparse-potential}\\
    \mathcal{K}_N&=-i[V_N,\,\cdot\,].\label{eq:sparse-Leps}
\end{align}
For a fixed $\varepsilon>0$, the perturbation $\varepsilon\mathcal{K}_N$ adds an on-site potential of strength $\varepsilon$ on the left and right thirds of the chain. Here $N$ is an auxiliary parameter used to set the physical chain length $m_N=\Theta(\log N)$. Both $\mathcal{L}_N$ and $\mathcal{L}_N+\varepsilon\mathcal{K}_N$ are primitive and have the unique fixed point $\tau_N=2^{-m}\mathbb{I}$. For every $0<\delta<1$ and, for the lower bound, $\ell\geq\max\{2,4J/\varepsilon\}$, we have
\begin{align}
    \tau_{\operatorname{mix}}^{\mathcal{L}_N}(\delta)
    &\leq\frac{9(m+1)^9}{2J}\left[\left(\frac m2+1\right)\log2+\log\frac1\delta\right],\label{eq:sparse-main-upper}\\
    \tau_{\operatorname{mix}}^{\mathcal{L}_N+\varepsilon\mathcal{K}_N}(1/2)
    &\geq\frac1{16J}\left(1+\frac\varepsilon{2J}\right)^{\ell-1}
    =N^{a\kappa_\varepsilon/3+o(1)},
    \qquad \kappa_\varepsilon=\log\left(1+\frac\varepsilon{2J}\right)>0.\label{eq:sparse-main-lower}
\end{align}
Hence $\mathcal{L}_N$ has polylogarithmic mixing time in $N$, whereas for every fixed $\varepsilon>0$, the mixing time of $\mathcal{L}_N+\varepsilon\mathcal{K}_N$ is bounded below by a positive power of $N$.
<!-- end example-5 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
\label{lemma:rm_MLSI} 
  \addcontentsline{toc}{subsection}{ 
    \texorpdfstring{\protect\cref*{lemma:rm_MLSI}}{Result \getrefnumber{lemma:rm_MLSI}}: Rapid mixing without MLSI} 

The Lindbladian family $(\mathcal{L}_N)_N$ defined by
\begin{align}
    \mathcal{L}_N(\rho)=\sum_{j=1}^N\bigl(-i[X_j,\rho]+\mathcal D[Z_j](\rho)\bigr)
\end{align}
has a unique full-rank fixed point $\mathbb{I}/2^N$ and is rapidly mixing with constant decay rate, but it does not have a positive MLSI constant.
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- lemma-8: body_md -->
\label{lem:commuting-unique-stationary} 
  \addcontentsline{toc}{subsubsection}{ 
    \texorpdfstring{\protect\cref*{lem:commuting-unique-stationary}}{Result \getrefnumber{lem:commuting-unique-stationary}}: Commuting addition to a relaxing generator} 

Let $\mathcal{L},\mathcal{K}$ be commuting Lindbladians and suppose that $\mathcal{L}$ has a unique stationary state $\sigma$ and a well-defined infinite-time limit. Then $\mathcal{K}(\sigma)=0$, $\mathcal{L}+\mathcal{K}$ has the unique stationary state $\sigma$, and, for every $\rho\in\mathcal{D}_1(\mathcal{H})$ and $t\ge0$,
\begin{align*}
    \|e^{t(\mathcal{L}+\mathcal{K})}(\rho)-\sigma\|_1\le \|e^{t\mathcal{L}}(\rho)-\sigma\|_1.
\end{align*}
In particular, every rapid-mixing bound for $\mathcal{L}$ is inherited by $\mathcal{L}+\mathcal{K}$.
<!-- end lemma-8 -->
<!-- lemma-9: body_md -->
\label{lem:commuting-kernel} 
  \addcontentsline{toc}{subsubsection}{ 
    \texorpdfstring{\protect\cref*{lem:commuting-kernel}}{Result \getrefnumber{lem:commuting-kernel}}: Commuting sum with kernel inclusion} 

Let $\mathcal{L},\mathcal{K}$ be commuting Lindbladians, suppose that $P_\mathcal{L}=\lim_{t\to\infty}e^{t\mathcal{L}}$ exists, and assume $\ker(\mathcal{L})\subseteq\ker(\mathcal{K})$. Then $P_{\mathcal{L}+\mathcal{K}}$ exists and equals $P_\mathcal{L}$, and for all $\rho\in\mathcal{D}_1(\mathcal{H})$ and all $t\ge0$,
\begin{align*}
    \|e^{t(\mathcal{L}+\mathcal{K})}(\rho)-P_{\mathcal{L}+\mathcal{K}}(\rho)\|_1\le \|e^{t\mathcal{L}}(\rho)-P_\mathcal{L}(\rho)\|_1.
\end{align*}
<!-- end lemma-9 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:commuting-stability} 
  \addcontentsline{toc}{subsubsection}{ 
    \texorpdfstring{\protect\cref*{prop:commuting-stability}}{Result \getrefnumber{prop:commuting-stability}}: Stability under commuting additions} 

Let $(\mathcal{L}_N)_N$ and $(\mathcal{K}_N)_N$ be Lindbladian families with $[\mathcal{L}_N,\mathcal{K}_N]=0$ for every $N$. If both families are rapidly mixing, then $(\mathcal{L}_N+\mathcal{K}_N)_N$ is rapidly mixing. If $(\mathcal{L}_N)_N$ is rapidly mixing and, for every $N$, $\mathcal{L}_N$ either has a unique stationary state or satisfies $\ker(\mathcal{L}_N)\subseteq\ker(\mathcal{K}_N)$, then its mixing bound is inherited by $(\mathcal{L}_N+\mathcal{K}_N)_N$.
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{prop:stability-strong-bulk-dissipation} 
  \addcontentsline{toc}{subsubsection}{ 
    \texorpdfstring{\protect\cref*{prop:stability-strong-bulk-dissipation}}{Result \getrefnumber{prop:stability-strong-bulk-dissipation}}: Stability of strong bulk dissipation} 

Let $(\mathcal{L}_N)_N$ be an $l$-local Lindbladian family with bulk-dissipative covers of uniformly bounded support size $a$ and incidence $\mathfrak d$, and local mixing time $t_{\mathrm{loc}}=O(1)$. Suppose that $\kappa_{\mathcal{L}_N}t_{\mathrm{loc}}\leq1/2-\Delta$ for some $\Delta>0$ independent of $N$. For every fixed locality $k$ and interaction-strength bound $s_{\mathcal{K}}$, there exists a constant $\varepsilon_*>0$, independent of $N$, such that, for every $k$-local Lindbladian family $(\mathcal{K}_N)_N$ with interaction strength at most $s_{\mathcal{K}}$, the family $(\mathcal{L}_N+\varepsilon\mathcal{K}_N)_N$ remains rapidly mixing with constant decay rate and has a unique stationary state for all $0\leq\varepsilon\leq\varepsilon_*$.
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{cor:commuting-strong-bulk-dissipation} 
  \addcontentsline{toc}{subsubsection}{ 
    \texorpdfstring{\protect\cref*{cor:commuting-strong-bulk-dissipation}}{Result \getrefnumber{cor:commuting-strong-bulk-dissipation}}: Commuting strong bulk dissipation} 

Let $(\mathcal{L}_N)_N$ be an $l$-local Lindbladian family whose local terms commute and contain bulk-dissipative covers of uniformly bounded support size $a$ and incidence $\mathfrak d$, and local mixing time $t_{\mathrm{loc}}=O(1)$. For every fixed locality $k$ and interaction-strength bound $s_{\mathcal{K}}$, there exists a constant $\varepsilon_*>0$, independent of $N$, such that, for every $k$-local Lindbladian family $(\mathcal{K}_N)_N$ with interaction strength at most $s_{\mathcal{K}}$, the family $(\mathcal{L}_N+\varepsilon\mathcal{K}_N)_N$ remains rapidly mixing with constant decay rate and has a unique stationary state for all $0\leq\varepsilon\leq\varepsilon_*$.
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\label{cor:main-gibbs-stability} 
  \addcontentsline{toc}{subsubsection}{ 
    \texorpdfstring{\protect\cref*{cor:main-gibbs-stability}}{Result \getrefnumber{cor:main-gibbs-stability}}: Stability of high-temperature Gibbs samplers} 

Let $(H_N)_N$ be a family of finite-range Hamiltonians on a $D$-dimensional qubit lattice, with uniformly bounded interaction strength and a uniformly bounded number of terms meeting each site. Let $(\mathcal{L}_N^{(\beta)})_N$ be the Gibbs sampler family of \cite{RouzeFrancaAlhambra2024b} with single-qubit Pauli bath couplings, at inverse temperature $\beta$. There exists a size-independent $\beta_*>0$ with the following property: for every $k$ and $s_{\mathcal{K}}$, there is a size-independent $\varepsilon_*>0$ such that, for every $k$-local Lindbladian perturbation family $(\mathcal{K}_N)_N$ with interaction strength at most $s_{\mathcal{K}}$, $(\mathcal{L}_N^{(\beta)}+\varepsilon\mathcal{K}_N)_N$ remains rapidly mixing with constant decay rate and has a unique stationary state whenever $0\leq\beta<\beta_*$ and $0\leq\varepsilon<\varepsilon_*$.
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
\label{cor:main-mpdo-stability} 
  \addcontentsline{toc}{subsubsection}{ 
    \texorpdfstring{\protect\cref*{cor:main-mpdo-stability}}{Result \getrefnumber{cor:main-mpdo-stability}}: Stability of simple injective MPDO parent dynamics} 

Consider the parent Lindbladian family $(\mathcal{L}_N)_N$ of \cite[Section~V~A]{liu2026parent} for a simple injective matrix product density operator at a renormalization fixed point on a periodic chain of $N\geq5$ sites. For every fixed $k$ and $s_{\mathcal{K}}$, there is a size-independent $\varepsilon_*>0$ such that, for $0\leq\varepsilon\leq\varepsilon_*$ and every $k$-local Lindbladian perturbation family $(\mathcal{K}_N)_N$ with interaction strength at most $s_{\mathcal{K}}$, $(\mathcal{L}_N+\varepsilon\mathcal{K}_N)_N$ remains rapidly mixing with constant decay rate and has a unique stationary state.
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
<!-- corollary-4: body_md -->
\label{cor:main-local-noise} 
  \addcontentsline{toc}{subsubsection}{ 
    \texorpdfstring{\protect\cref*{cor:main-local-noise}}{Result \getrefnumber{cor:main-local-noise}}: Loss of long-range order under strong local noise} 

Let $(\mathcal{L}_N)_N$ and $(\mathcal{N}_N)_N$, with $\mathcal{N}_N=\sum_B\mathcal{N}_B$, be geometrically local Lindbladian families on a fixed-dimensional lattice, both with uniformly bounded per-site interaction strength. Suppose that the supports of the noise terms have uniformly bounded size and incidence and cover the lattice. Suppose each $\mathcal{N}_B$ has a unique local stationary state and a common local mixing time bound $t_{\mathrm{noise}}=O(1)$. Let $\kappa_{\mathcal{N}}$ be defined by \cref{eq:main-local-influence} for the cover consisting of the noise terms. Assume that $\kappa_{\mathcal{N}}t_{\mathrm{noise}}\leq1/2-\Delta$ for a size-independent $\Delta>0$. Then there exists a size-independent $\varepsilon_*>0$ such that, for every fixed $\varepsilon>\varepsilon_*$, the family $(\mathcal{L}_N+\varepsilon\mathcal{N}_N)_N$ has a unique stationary state and is rapidly mixing with constant decay rate. The influence condition is always satisfied when the noise terms commute.
<!-- end corollary-4 -->
<!-- definition-6: body_md -->
The Lindbladian
\begin{align*}
    \mathcal{L}(\rho)=-i[H,\rho]+\sum_\mu\left(2L_\mu\rho L_\mu^\dagger-\{L_\mu^\dagger L_\mu,\rho\}\right)
\end{align*}
is called \emph{quasifree} if $H$ is quadratic in the Majorana operators and $L_\mu$ are linear:
\begin{align*}
    H=\frac{i}{4}\sum_{j,k=1}^m \mathbf{H}_{j,k}c_jc_k,\qquad L_\mu=\sum_{j=1}^m l_{\mu,j}c_j,
\end{align*}
where $\mathbf{H}=-\mathbf{H}^T\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}$.
<!-- end definition-6 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{cor:sum-gaussian} 
  \addcontentsline{toc}{subsubsection}{ 
    \texorpdfstring{\protect\cref*{cor:sum-gaussian}}{Result \getrefnumber{cor:sum-gaussian}}: Stability under quasifree additions} 

Let $(\mathcal{L}_N)_N$ be a quasifree fermionic Lindbladian family on $N$ fermionic modes, with $\operatorname{Re}(\mathbf M_{\mathcal{L}_N})\succeq\mu\mathbb{I}$ for some $\mu>0$ independent of $N$. For every quasifree Lindbladian family $(\mathcal{K}_N)_N$ on the same modes, $(\mathcal{L}_N+\mathcal{K}_N)_N$ is rapidly mixing with constant decay rate and a unique stationary state.
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
\label{prop:qf-translation-invariant-stability} 
  \addcontentsline{toc}{subsubsection}{ 
    \texorpdfstring{\protect\cref*{prop:qf-translation-invariant-stability}}{Result \getrefnumber{prop:qf-translation-invariant-stability}}: Translation-invariant quasifree stability under perturbations} 

Let $(\mathcal{L}_N)_N$ be a translation-invariant quasifree Lindbladian family on periodic lattices $\Lambda_N=(\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z)^D$, with one fermionic mode per unit cell and uniformly bounded interaction strength $s_{\mathcal{L}}$. Let $\mathbf X_{\mathcal{L}_N}$ be its single-particle matrix. Suppose that for some $\gamma>0$, independently of $N$,
\begin{align}
    \max_{z\in\operatorname{spec}(\mathbf X_{\mathcal{L}_N})}\operatorname{Re}z&\leq-\gamma\qquad\text{for every }N, \label{eq:qf-ti-symbol-gap}
\end{align}
Then:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[a)] The family $(\mathcal{L}_N)_N$ is rapidly mixing with constant decay rate.
\item[b)] For every interaction-strength bound $s_{\mathcal{K}}$, there exists a constant $\varepsilon_*>0$, independent of $N$, such that, for every quasifree Lindbladian family $(\mathcal{K}_N)_N$ with interaction strength at most $s_{\mathcal{K}}$, not necessarily translation invariant, the family $(\mathcal{L}_N+\varepsilon\mathcal{K}_N)_N$ remains rapidly mixing with constant decay rate for all $0\leq\varepsilon\leq\varepsilon_*$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- proposition-5: body_md -->
\label{thm:CE}
Assume $e^{t\mathcal{L}}$ has a full-rank invariant state $\sigma$. Then there is a unique conditional expectation $E^*_\mathcal{L}:\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H})\to\mathcal{F}(\mathcal{L})$ with $E_\mathcal{L}(\sigma)=\sigma$, and for every $X\in\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H})$,
\begin{align*}
    \lim_{t\to+\infty}e^{t\mathcal{L}^*}(X-E^*_\mathcal{L}[X])=0, \qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad \lim_{t\to+\infty}e^{t\mathcal{L}}(\rho-E_\mathcal{L}(\rho))=0\quad\forall\rho\in\mathcal{D}_1(\mathcal{H}).
\end{align*}
If $\mathcal{L}$ has no nonzero purely imaginary eigenvalues, then $E_\mathcal{L}=P_\mathcal{L}$.
<!-- end proposition-5 -->
<!-- proposition-6: body_md -->
\label{prop:mlsi-commuting} 
  \addcontentsline{toc}{subsubsection}{ 
    \texorpdfstring{\protect\cref*{prop:mlsi-commuting}}{Result \getrefnumber{prop:mlsi-commuting}}: MLSI for commuting stationary projections} 

Let $\mathcal{H}$ be a finite-dimensional Hilbert space, and let $\mathcal{L}$ and $\mathcal{K}$ be Lindbladians on $\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H})$, each with a full-rank invariant state, a well-defined infinite-time limit, and a positive MLSI constant. Suppose that
\begin{align*}
    E_\mathcal{L} E_\mathcal{K}=E_\mathcal{K} E_\mathcal{L}.
\end{align*}
Then the infinite-time limit of $\mathcal{L}+\mathcal{K}$ exists, and
\begin{align}
    E_{\mathcal{L}+\mathcal{K}}=E_\mathcal{L} E_\mathcal{K},\qquad
    \ker(\mathcal{L}+\mathcal{K})=\ker\mathcal{L}\cap\ker\mathcal{K},\qquad
    \alpha(\mathcal{L}+\mathcal{K})\geq\min\{\alpha(\mathcal{L}),\alpha(\mathcal{K})\}.
\end{align}
If $E_\mathcal{L}=E_\mathcal{K}$, the stronger bound
\begin{align*}
    \alpha(\mathcal{L}+\mathcal{K})\geq\alpha(\mathcal{L})+\alpha(\mathcal{K})
\end{align*}
holds.
<!-- end proposition-6 -->
<!-- proposition-7: body_md -->
\label{prop:mlsi-kernel} 
  \addcontentsline{toc}{subsubsection}{ 
    \texorpdfstring{\protect\cref*{prop:mlsi-kernel}}{Result \getrefnumber{prop:mlsi-kernel}}: MLSI under kernel inclusion} 

Let $\mathcal{L}$ be a Lindbladian with a full-rank invariant state, a well-defined infinite-time limit $E_\mathcal{L}$, and $\alpha(\mathcal{L})>0$. Let $\mathcal{K}$ be a Lindbladian satisfying $\ker\mathcal{L}\subseteq\ker\mathcal{K}$. Then the infinite-time limit of $\mathcal{L}+\mathcal{K}$ exists, and
\begin{align*}
    E_{\mathcal{L}+\mathcal{K}}=E_\mathcal{L},\qquad
    \ker(\mathcal{L}+\mathcal{K})=\ker\mathcal{L},\qquad
    \alpha(\mathcal{L}+\mathcal{K})\geq\alpha(\mathcal{L}).
\end{align*}
<!-- end proposition-7 -->
<!-- proposition-8: body_md -->
\label{prop:tkrw-stability} 
  \addcontentsline{toc}{subsubsection}{ 
    \texorpdfstring{\protect\cref*{prop:tkrw-stability}}{Result \getrefnumber{prop:tkrw-stability}}: Stability of the \texorpdfstring{$\chi^2$}{chi-squared} mixing bound} 

Let $\mathcal L$ and $\mathcal K$ be Lindbladians satisfying $\mathcal L(\sigma)=\mathcal K(\sigma)=0$ for the same state $\sigma\succ0$. For every $k\in K$, using this same $\sigma$ to define all three operators, we have
\begin{align*}
    \Lambda_k(\mathcal L+\mathcal K)&=\Lambda_k(\mathcal L)+\Lambda_k(\mathcal K)\preceq\Lambda_k(\mathcal L),\\
    l_1^k(\mathcal L+\mathcal K)&\le l_1^k(\mathcal L)+l_1^k(\mathcal K).
\end{align*}
If $l_1^k(\mathcal L)+l_1^k(\mathcal K)<0$, then $\mathcal L+\mathcal K$ converges exponentially to $\sigma$, which is therefore its unique stationary state.
<!-- end proposition-8 -->
<!-- conjecture-1: body_md -->
\label{conj:uniform-rm-instability}
There exist geometrically local Lindbladian families $(\mathcal{L}_N)_N$ and $(\mathcal{K}_N)_N$ on lattices of $N$ sites, with range and local interaction strength bounded independently of $N$, and a constant $\varepsilon_*>0$, such that $(\mathcal{L}_N)_N$ is uniformly rapidly mixing, but $(\mathcal{L}_N+\varepsilon\mathcal{K}_N)_N$ has a well-defined infinite-time limit and is not rapidly mixing for every fixed $0<\varepsilon<\varepsilon_*$. The two families are fixed independently of $\varepsilon$.\footnote{The boundary-dissipation example in \cref{ex:sparse-boundary-potential} does not furnish a uniformly rapidly mixing family of this kind. The distance between dissipation sites grows with $N$, leaving arbitrarily large interior regions whose restricted dynamics is purely Hamiltonian.}
<!-- end conjecture-1 -->
<!-- example-6: body_md -->
\label{app:ex:XZeps}
On a spin chain of $N$ sites, write $\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_N$ and $\mathcal{K}=\mathcal{K}_N$ for the local generators of the families $(\mathcal{L}_N)_N$ and $(\mathcal{K}_N)_N$, with jump operator $Z_j$ at every site $j$ and Hamiltonians $X_j$ and $(\varepsilon_j-1)X_j$, respectively:
\begin{align}
    \mathcal{L}(\rho)=\sum_j\bigl(-i[X_j,\rho]+\mathcal D[Z_j](\rho)\bigr),\qquad \mathcal{K}(\rho)=\sum_j\bigl(-i[(\varepsilon_j-1)X_j,\rho]+\mathcal D[Z_j](\rho)\bigr),
\end{align}
where $\varepsilon_j= 1/(j+1)$. Both generators have the unique full-rank fixed point $\sigma=(\mathbb{I}/2)^{\otimes N}$, and both families are rapidly mixing. For every finite $N$, the sum $\mathcal{L}+\mathcal{K}$ is primitive and gapped, but its gap is $\Theta(N^{-2})$ and its mixing time is $\Omega(N^2)$, so $(\mathcal{L}_N+\mathcal{K}_N)_N$ is not rapidly mixing.
<!-- end example-6 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
\renewcommand{\getrefnumber{#1}}{\getrefnumber{lem:XZeps}} 
  \refstepcounter{proof} 
  \label{proof:XZeps} 

We first prove rapid mixing of the two summands by obtaining a single-site mixing bound that is uniform in $j$ and then telescoping the tensor-product channels. We then compute the gap of their sum and use its slowest mode to rule out rapid mixing.

\emph{Rapid mixing of each summand.} For a single qubit, write
\begin{align}
    \mathcal G_{h,d}(\rho)&=-ih[X,\rho]+d\mathcal D[Z](\rho),\qquad d>0.
\end{align}
The generator fixes $\mathbb{I}/2$. Using $[X,Y]=2iZ$, $[X,Z]=-2iY$, $ZXZ=-X$, and $ZYZ=-Y$, its action on the traceless Pauli basis is
\begin{align}
    \mathcal G_{h,d}(X)&=-2dX,\notag\\
    \mathcal G_{h,d}(Y)&=-2dY+2hZ,\notag\\
    \mathcal G_{h,d}(Z)&=-2hY.
\end{align}
Thus its matrix on $(X,Y,Z)$ and its characteristic polynomial are
\begin{align}
    A_{h,d}&=\begin{pmatrix}-2d&0&0\\
    0&-2d&-2h\\
    0&2h&0\end{pmatrix},\notag\\
    \det(z\mathbb{I}-A_{h,d})&=(z+2d)(z^2+2dz+4h^2).
\end{align}
The eigenvalues on the traceless subspace are consequently
\begin{align}
    \operatorname{spec}(A_{h,d})&=\{-2d,-d\pm\sqrt{d^2-4h^2}\}. \label{eq:XZeps-single-site-spectrum}
\end{align}
For $h\ne0$, all three eigenvalues have strictly negative real part: if $d^2-4h^2\geq0$, then $\sqrt{d^2-4h^2}<d$, while otherwise the two roots have real part $-d$. Hence $\mathcal G_{h,d}$ is primitive with unique stationary state $\mathbb{I}/2$.

The single-site terms of $\mathcal{L}$ and $\mathcal{K}$ have $d=1$ and respectively $h=1$ and $h=\varepsilon_j-1=-j/(j+1)$, so in both cases $1/2\leq|h|\leq1$. We need a mixing bound uniform in this range, including $|h|=1/2$, where the two eigenvalues of the $(Y,Z)$ block coincide. Write this block as $-\mathbb{I}+B_h$, with
\begin{align}
    B_h&=\begin{pmatrix}-1&-2h\\
    2h&1\end{pmatrix}, & B_h^2&=-(4h^2-1)\mathbb{I}.
\end{align}
The diagonal and off-diagonal parts have norms $1$ and $2|h|$, respectively, so $\|B_h\|\leq1+2|h|\leq3$. Set $\omega_h=\sqrt{4h^2-1}$. Expanding the exponential into its even and odd powers gives
\begin{align}
    \bigl\|e^{t(-\mathbb{I}+B_h)}\bigr\| &\overset{(1)}{=}e^{-t}\left\|\cos(\omega_ht)\mathbb{I}+ \frac{\sin(\omega_ht)}{\omega_h}B_h\right\|,\notag\\
    &\overset{(2)}{\leq}e^{-t}\left(|\cos(\omega_ht)|+ \left|\frac{\sin(\omega_ht)}{\omega_h}\right|\|B_h\|\right),\notag\\
    &\overset{(3)}{\leq}(1+3t)e^{-t}, \label{eq:XZeps-block-decay}
\end{align}
where $(1)$ uses $B_h^2=-\omega_h^2\mathbb{I}$ and commutativity with the identity, $(2)$ is the triangle inequality, and $(3)$ uses $|\cos(\omega_ht)|\leq1$, $|\sin(\omega_ht)|\leq\omega_ht$, and $\|B_h\|\leq3$. At $\omega_h=0$, the quotient is interpreted by continuity as $t$, and the same estimate holds.

Let $P(O)=\tfrac12\operatorname{Tr}(O)\mathbb{I}$. The map $e^{t\mathcal G_{h,1}}-P$ vanishes on the identity and has matrix $e^{tA_{h,1}}$ on the traceless Pauli basis. Since the space of single-qubit linear maps has fixed dimension, equivalence of norms gives a constant $C_0$, independent of $h,j,N$, such that
\begin{align}
    \|e^{t\mathcal G_{h,1}}-P\|_\diamond &\overset{(1)}{\leq}C_0\|e^{tA_{h,1}}\|,\notag\\
    &\overset{(2)}{\leq}C_0(1+3t)e^{-t},\notag\\
    &\overset{(3)}{\leq}Ce^{-t/2}, \label{eq:XZeps-local-mixing}
\end{align}
where $(1)$ is this norm comparison in the fixed Pauli basis, $(2)$ uses \cref{eq:XZeps-block-decay} and the decay $e^{-2t}$ on $X$, and $(3)$ uses $C:=C_0\sup_{s\geq0}(1+3s)e^{-s/2}<\infty$.

For either choice of the summand, let $T_{j,t}$ be its single-site channel. The tensor-product difference has the telescoping expansion
\begin{align}
    \bigotimes_{j=1}^NT_{j,t}-P^{\otimes N} &=\sum_{j=1}^NP^{\otimes(j-1)}\otimes(T_{j,t}-P) \otimes\bigotimes_{k=j+1}^NT_{k,t}.
\end{align}
Therefore
\begin{align}
    \left\|\bigotimes_{j=1}^NT_{j,t}-P^{\otimes N}\right\|_\diamond &\overset{(1)}{\leq}\sum_{j=1}^N \left\|P^{\otimes(j-1)}\otimes(T_{j,t}-P) \otimes\bigotimes_{k=j+1}^NT_{k,t}\right\|_\diamond,\notag\\
    &\overset{(2)}{\leq}\sum_{j=1}^N\|T_{j,t}-P\|_\diamond,\notag\\
    &\overset{(3)}{\leq}CNe^{-t/2},
\end{align}
where $(1)$ is the triangle inequality applied to the telescoping expansion, $(2)$ uses multiplicativity of the diamond norm and the fact that $P,T_{k,t}$ are channels with diamond norm one, and $(3)$ uses \cref{eq:XZeps-local-mixing}. Since $P^{\otimes N}(\rho)=\sigma=(\mathbb{I}/2)^{\otimes N}$ for every state $\rho$, this proves rapid mixing with constant decay rate for both $\mathcal{L}$ and $\mathcal{K}$ towards $\sigma$. Stationarity follows from the single-site calculation, and convergence to $\sigma$ proves uniqueness. Both generators are unital and $\sigma$ is full rank.

\emph{Closing gap of the sum.} The Hamiltonian terms add to $\varepsilon_jX_j$, while the dephasing strength doubles:
\begin{align}
    (\mathcal{L}+\mathcal{K})(\rho) &=\sum_{j=1}^N\bigl(-i[\varepsilon_jX_j,\rho]+2\mathcal D[Z_j](\rho)\bigr).
\end{align}
Its single-site generator is $\mathcal G_{\varepsilon_j,2}$. Substituting $h=\varepsilon_j$ and $d=2$ into \cref{eq:XZeps-single-site-spectrum} gives the nonzero eigenvalues
\begin{align}
    -4,\qquad -2\pm2\sqrt{1-\varepsilon_j^2}.
\end{align}
They are strictly negative because $0<\varepsilon_j\leq1/2$. Hence the sum is primitive for every finite $N$, with the same stationary state $\sigma$. Since the single-site generators act on different tensor factors, the full spectrum consists of sums of their eigenvalues. Its gap is thus
\begin{align}
    g_N:=\operatorname{gap}(\mathcal{L}+\mathcal{K}) &\overset{(1)}{=}\min_{1\leq j\leq N}2\left(1-\sqrt{1-\varepsilon_j^2}\right),\notag\\
    &\overset{(2)}{=}2\left(1-\sqrt{1-\varepsilon_N^2}\right),\notag\\
    &\overset{(3)}{=}\frac{2\varepsilon_N^2}{1+\sqrt{1-\varepsilon_N^2}} \overset{(4)}{=}\Theta(N^{-2}), \label{eq:XZeps-sum-gap}
\end{align}
where $(1)$ uses the tensor-sum spectrum and the smallest single-site decay rate, $(2)$ uses that $\varepsilon_j=1/(j+1)$ decreases with $j$ and $x\mapsto1-\sqrt{1-x^2}$ increases on $(0,1)$, $(3)$ rationalizes the numerator, and $(4)$ uses $\varepsilon_N=(N+1)^{-1}$ and $1\leq1+\sqrt{1-\varepsilon_N^2}\leq2$.

We finally check explicitly why this closing gap rules out rapid mixing. The real $(Y,Z)$ block of $\mathcal G_{\varepsilon_N,2}$ has a real eigenvector with eigenvalue $-g_N$. Its corresponding Pauli combination gives a traceless Hermitian eigenoperator $F_N$, which we normalize by $\|F_N\|=1$. Its two eigenvalues are then $1$ and $-1$, so $(\mathbb{I}+F_N)/2$ is a state and $\|F_N\|_1=2$. Choose the initial state
\begin{align}
    \rho_N&=(\mathbb{I}/2)^{\otimes(N-1)}\otimes(\mathbb{I}+F_N)/2.
\end{align}
Only the last site evolves away from its stationary state, and
\begin{align}
    \|e^{t(\mathcal{L}+\mathcal{K})}(\rho_N)-\sigma\|_1 &\overset{(1)}{=}\left\|(\mathbb{I}/2)^{\otimes(N-1)}\otimes \tfrac12 e^{t\mathcal G_{\varepsilon_N,2}}(F_N)\right\|_1,\notag\\
    &\overset{(2)}{=}\tfrac12e^{-g_Nt} \left\|(\mathbb{I}/2)^{\otimes(N-1)}\right\|_1\|F_N\|_1,\notag\\
    &\overset{(3)}{=}e^{-g_Nt},
\end{align}
where $(1)$ uses the tensor-product evolution, stationarity of $\mathbb{I}/2$, and linearity, $(2)$ uses the eigenoperator equation and multiplicativity of the trace norm, and $(3)$ uses that a state has trace norm one and $\|F_N\|_1=2$. Therefore
\begin{align}
    \tau_{\operatorname{mix}}^{\mathcal{L}+\mathcal{K}}(1/2)\geq\frac{\log2}{g_N}=\Omega(N^2),
\end{align}
which rules out rapid mixing under \cref{eq:rapid-mixing-time}.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- example-7: body_md -->
\label{app:ex:fermionic-addition}
For odd $N\geq5$, let $\Lambda_N=\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z$, with two fermionic annihilation operators $a_x,b_x$ in each cell $x$. With indices understood modulo $N$, define
\begin{align}
    H_{\lambda,N}&=\sum_{x\in\Lambda_N}\left[\lambda a_x^\dagger b_x+\frac12(a_{x+1}^\dagger+a_{x-1}^\dagger)b_x+\mathrm{h.c.}\right],\label{eq:fermionic-addition-H}\\
    \mathcal{L}_{\lambda,N}(\rho)&=-i[H_{\lambda,N},\rho]+\sum_{x\in\Lambda_N}\left(\mathcal D[a_x](\rho)+\mathcal D[a_x^\dagger](\rho)\right).\label{eq:fermionic-addition-L}
\end{align}
Define the families $(\mathcal{L}_N^\pm)_N$ and $(\mathcal S_N)_N$ by $\mathcal{L}_N^\pm=\mathcal{L}_{\pm2,N}$ and $\mathcal S_N=\mathcal{L}_N^++\mathcal{L}_N^-$, and set $\sigma_N=4^{-N}\mathbb{I}$. Then
\begin{align}
    \lVert e^{t\mathcal{L}_N^\pm}-P_{\mathcal{L}_N^\pm}\rVert_\diamond\leq12Ne^{-t/2},\qquad P_{\mathcal{L}_N^\pm}(X)=\operatorname{Tr}(X)\sigma_N.\label{eq:fermionic-addition-individual}
\end{align}
The same estimate, with $N$ replaced by $|A|$, holds for the restriction to every nonempty set of cells $A$, retaining the on-site jumps and the Hamiltonian terms supported in $A$. The sum $\mathcal S_N=2\mathcal{L}_{0,N}$ is primitive with fixed point $\sigma_N$, but
\begin{align}
    \tau_{\operatorname{mix}}^{\mathcal S_N}(\varepsilon)&\geq\frac{\log(\varepsilon^{-1})}{2r_N}
    \geq\frac{N^2}{2\pi^2}\log(\varepsilon^{-1}),
    &r_N&=1-\sqrt{1-4\sin^2\left(\frac{\pi}{2N}\right)}.\label{eq:fermionic-addition-lower}
\end{align}
The state establishing this bound has even parity.
<!-- end example-7 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
\renewcommand{\getrefnumber{#1}}{\getrefnumber{lem:fermionic-addition}} 
  \refstepcounter{proof} 
  \label{proof:fermionic-addition} 

We verify the claims for the construction in \cref{ex:fermionic-addition}.

\emph{Uniform rapid mixing of the summands.} For $q_k=2\pi k/N$, define
\begin{align}
    a_k=N^{-1/2}\sum_xe^{-iq_kx}a_x,\qquad b_k=N^{-1/2}\sum_xe^{-iq_kx}b_x.
\end{align}
Unitary mixing of the jump list leaves the dissipator invariant, and therefore
\begin{align}
    H_{\lambda,N}&=\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}g_\lambda(q_k)(a_k^\dagger b_k+b_k^\dagger a_k),
    &g_\lambda(q)&=\lambda+\cos q,\notag\\
    \sum_x(\mathcal D[a_x]+\mathcal D[a_x^\dagger])&=\sum_k(\mathcal D[a_k]+\mathcal D[a_k^\dagger]).
\end{align}
With $\Pi$ as in \cref{eq:qf-parity-dressing}, for $a=(c_1+ic_2)/2$ one has $\mathcal D[a]+\mathcal D[a^\dagger]=\tfrac12(\mathcal D[c_1]+\mathcal D[c_2])$, so the generators are unital. More generally, if the balanced gain and loss term has coefficient $\kappa>0$, the matrix governing the evolution of the linear observables in the dressed basis $(i\Pi a_k,i\Pi b_k)$ is
\begin{align}
    B_\kappa(g)&=\begin{pmatrix}-\kappa&-ig\\-ig&0\end{pmatrix},
    &z_\pm(g)&=-\frac\kappa2\pm\sqrt{\frac{\kappa^2}{4}-g^2}.\label{eq:fermionic-addition-drift}
\end{align}
For $\lambda=\pm2$, $1\leq|g_\lambda(q)|\leq3$. With $\kappa=1$ and $\omega_g=\sqrt{g^2-1/4}$,
\begin{align}
    e^{tB_1(g)}&=e^{-t/2}\left[\cos(\omega_gt)\mathbb{I}+\frac{\sin(\omega_gt)}{\omega_g}\left(B_1(g)+\tfrac12\mathbb{I}\right)\right],\notag\\
    \lVert e^{tB_1(g)}\rVert&\leq e^{-t/2}\left(1+\frac{|g|+1/2}{\sqrt{g^2-1/4}}\right)\leq3e^{-t/2}.
\end{align}
There are $4N$ Majoranas, so \cref{eq:fermionic-clifford-bound} gives \cref{eq:fermionic-addition-individual}, which proves primitivity and rapid mixing with constant decay rate.

For a restriction to cells $A$, define the real symmetric matrix
\begin{align}
    (J_A)_{xy}:=\frac12\mathbf1\bigl[\{x,y\}\text{ is an edge of the subgraph induced by }A\bigr],\qquad x,y\in A.
\end{align}
It satisfies $\lVert J_A\rVert\leq1$: the sum of the absolute values in each row is at most one, and $J_A$ is symmetric. Write $J_A=U_A\operatorname{diag}(\nu_1,\ldots,\nu_{|A|})U_A^T$, where $U_A$ is real orthogonal and $|\nu_j|\leq1$. Define modes
\begin{align*}
    \widetilde a_j&=\sum_{x\in A}(U_A)_{xj}a_x,\qquad
    \widetilde b_j=\sum_{x\in A}(U_A)_{xj}b_x.
\end{align*}
The same change of basis on both species diagonalizes the restricted hopping matrix $\pm2\mathbb{I}+J_A$. Thus
\begin{align*}
    H_{\pm2,A}&=\sum_{j=1}^{|A|}(\pm2+\nu_j)
    (\widetilde a_j^\dagger\widetilde b_j+\widetilde b_j^\dagger\widetilde a_j).
\end{align*}
Orthogonality gives $\sum_j(U_A)_{xj}(U_A)_{yj}=\delta_{xy}$, so expanding both the jump and anticommutator terms yields
\begin{align*}
    \sum_{x\in A}(\mathcal D[a_x]+\mathcal D[a_x^\dagger])
    &=\sum_{j=1}^{|A|}(\mathcal D[\widetilde a_j]+\mathcal D[\widetilde a_j^\dagger]).
\end{align*}
The restricted drift therefore has blocks $B_1(\pm2+\nu_j)$ and their complex conjugates. Since $1\leq|\pm2+\nu_j|\leq3$, the bound above gives $\|e^{t\mathbf X_A}\|\leq3e^{-t/2}$, independently of the shape or connectedness of $A$. There are $4|A|$ Majoranas, and \cref{eq:fermionic-clifford-bound} now gives
\begin{align*}
    \|e^{t\mathcal{L}_A^\pm}-P_{\mathcal{L}_A^\pm}\|_\diamond
    &\leq12|A|e^{-t/2},\qquad
    P_{\mathcal{L}_A^\pm}(X)=4^{-|A|}\operatorname{Tr}(X)\mathbb{I}.
\end{align*}
This proves uniform rapid mixing with constant decay rate.

\emph{Slow mixing of the sum.} Adding the two generators cancels the on-site hopping and doubles the intercell hopping and the dissipator. Thus the matrices governing the linear-observable evolution are
\begin{align}
    B^{\mathrm{sum}}(q)=2B_1(\cos q)=\begin{pmatrix}-2&-2i\cos q\\-2i\cos q&0\end{pmatrix},
\end{align}
with eigenvalues $-1\pm\sqrt{1-4\cos^2q}$. Since $N$ is odd,
\begin{align}
    \min_k|\cos q_k|=\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2N}\right)>0.
\end{align}
Every eigenvalue of $B^{\mathrm{sum}}(q_k)$ has strictly negative real part, so \cref{eq:fermionic-clifford-bound} gives convergence to the full-rank state $\sigma_N$ and hence primitivity of $\mathcal S_N$.

It remains to produce an even slow mode. Let $k_*\in\arg\min_k|\cos q_k|$, write $f=(a_{k_*},b_{k_*})^T$, and choose a unit eigenvector $w$ of $(B^{\mathrm{sum}}(q_{k_*}))^\dagger$ with eigenvalue $-r_N$. For a Hermitian $2\times2$ matrix $Q$, put
\begin{align}
    O_Q=f^\dagger Qf-\frac12\operatorname{Tr}(Q)\mathbb{I}.
\end{align}
To verify its evolution, write $B=-ih-2P_a$, where $h=2\cos(q_{k_*})\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ and $P_a=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)$. The CAR give the Hamiltonian contribution
\begin{align}
    i[H,f^\dagger Qf]&=f^\dagger i[h,Q]f,
\end{align}
while direct substitution in the balanced gain and loss dissipator gives
\begin{align}
    2(\mathcal D[a_{k_*}]+\mathcal D[a_{k_*}^\dagger])^*(f^\dagger Qf)
    &=-2f^\dagger(P_aQ+QP_a)f+2\operatorname{Tr}(P_aQ)\mathbb{I}.
\end{align}
Combining the two identities and centering by $\operatorname{Tr}(Q)/2$ yields
\begin{align}
    \mathcal S_N^*(O_Q)=O_{B^\dagger Q+QB},\qquad B=B^{\mathrm{sum}}(q_{k_*}).
\end{align}
Taking $Q=ww^\dagger$ and $W=2O_Q$ yields $W=W^\dagger$, $W^2=\mathbb{I}$, $\operatorname{Tr} W=0$, and $\mathcal S_N^*(W)=-2r_NW$. The state $\rho_N=\sigma_N(\mathbb{I}+W)$ is positive, normalized, and has even parity. Trace-norm duality gives
\begin{align}
    \lVert e^{t\mathcal S_N}(\rho_N)-\sigma_N\rVert_1
    &\geq\left|\operatorname{Tr}\left[W(e^{t\mathcal S_N}(\rho_N)-\sigma_N)\right]\right|=e^{-2r_Nt}.
\end{align}
Finally, with $s=\sin(\pi/(2N))<1/2$,
\begin{align}
    2s^2\leq r_N=\frac{4s^2}{1+\sqrt{1-4s^2}}\leq4s^2\leq\frac{\pi^2}{N^2}.
\end{align}
This proves \cref{eq:fermionic-addition-lower} and completes the proof.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- lemma-10: body_md -->
\label{app:lemma:rm_MLSI}
The Lindbladian family $(\mathcal{L}_N)_N$ defined by
\begin{align}
    \mathcal{L}_N(\rho)=\sum_{j=1}^N\bigl(-i[X_j,\rho]+\mathcal D[Z_j](\rho)\bigr)
\end{align}
has the unique full-rank fixed point $\mathbb{I}/2^N$ and is rapidly mixing with constant decay rate, but it does not have a positive MLSI constant.
<!-- end lemma-10 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
\renewcommand{\getrefnumber{#1}}{\getrefnumber{lemma:rm_MLSI}} 
  \refstepcounter{proof} 
  \label{proof:rm_MLSI} 

Rapid mixing with constant decay rate and the unique full-rank stationary state $\sigma=2^{-N}\mathbb{I}$ follow from \cref{ex:XZeps}, proved in \cref{proof:XZeps}. It remains to show that $\mathcal{L}$ has no positive MLSI constant. Write $\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_N=\sum_{j=1}^N\mathcal{L}_j$, where $\mathcal{L}_j(\rho)=-i[X_j,\rho]+\mathcal D[Z_j](\rho)$.

Let $\omega=\frac12(\mathbb{I}+cZ)$ with $c\in(-1,0)\cup(0,1)$ and $\rho=\omega^{\otimes N}$. The entropy production of $\rho$ is
\begin{align}
    \operatorname{EP}(\rho)=-\operatorname{Tr}[\mathcal{L}(\rho)(\log\rho-\log(2^{-N}\mathbb{I}))] =-\operatorname{Tr}[\mathcal{L}(\rho)\log\rho],
\end{align}
since $\mathcal{L}(\rho)$ is traceless and $\log(2^{-N}\mathbb{I})$ is a multiple of $\mathbb{I}$. Using $\mathcal{L}(\omega^{\otimes N})=\sum_{j=1}^N\omega^{\otimes\hat j}\otimes\mathcal{L}_j(\omega)$, where $\omega^{\otimes\hat j}$ denotes the tensor product over all sites except $j$, we get:
\begin{align*}
    \operatorname{EP}(\rho) &=\sum_{j=1}^N-\operatorname{Tr}\bigl[(\omega^{\otimes\hat j}\otimes\mathcal{L}_j(\omega)) \log(\omega^{\otimes N})\bigr],\\
    &=\sum_{j=1}^N-\operatorname{Tr}_j[\mathcal{L}_j(\omega)\log\omega],
\end{align*}
where in the last expression we expand the logarithm $\log(A\otimes B)=\log A\otimes\mathbb{I}+\mathbb{I}\otimes\log B$ and notice that the cross terms vanish because $\operatorname{Tr}_j(\mathcal{L}_j(\omega))=0$. For the single-site state $\omega$, the dissipative term vanishes because $Z\omega Z=\omega$, so $\mathcal{L}_j(\omega)=-i[X,\omega]=-cY$, while $\log\omega=d_1\mathbb{I}+d_2Z$ for $d_1=\frac12\log\frac{1-c^2}{4}$, $d_2=\frac12\log\frac{1+c}{1-c}$; hence
\begin{align*}
    \operatorname{Tr}_j[\mathcal{L}_j(\omega)\log\omega] =\operatorname{Tr}[-cY(d_1\mathbb{I}+d_2Z)]=0,
\end{align*}
because $\operatorname{Tr} Y=0=\operatorname{Tr}(YZ)$. Thus $\operatorname{EP}(\rho)=0$. On the other hand $\rho\ne2^{-N}\mathbb{I}$, so by Klein's inequality $D(\rho\|2^{-N}\mathbb{I})>0$. Hence no positive $\alpha$ can satisfy the MLSI $2\alpha D(\rho\|2^{-N}\mathbb{I})\le \operatorname{EP}(\rho)$ for such $\rho$.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- example-8: body_md -->
\label{app:ex:ising-kernel-mismatch}
Let $\Lambda_L=\{1,\ldots,L\}^2$, with free boundary conditions, even $L\geq4$, and $N=L^2$, and let
\begin{align}
    H_L=-\sum_{\langle x,y\rangle}Z_xZ_y, \qquad \sigma_{\beta,L}=\frac{e^{-\beta H_L}}{\operatorname{Tr} e^{-\beta H_L}}
\end{align}
be the Hamiltonian and Gibbs state of the two-dimensional Ising model.
There are two geometrically 5-local, zero-Hamiltonian families $(\mathcal{L}_{1,N})_N$ and $(\mathcal{L}_{2,N})_N$, written $\mathcal{L}_i=\mathcal{L}_{i,N}$ at each size, with the following properties:
\begin{enumerate}
\item each has $\sigma_{\beta,L}$ as a full rank fixed state, satisfies the fixed-point MLSI with a constant at least $1/2$, and obeys
\begin{align}
    \label{eq:app-ising-layer-rm} \sup_\rho\|e^{t\mathcal{L}_i}(\rho)-P_{\mathcal{L}_i}(\rho)\|_1 \leq 2N e^{-t},\qquad i\in\{1,2\};
\end{align}
\item their fixed-point spaces are different and strictly larger than the span of $\sigma_{\beta,L}$;
\item for every sufficiently large fixed $\beta$ and all sufficiently large $L$, their sum is primitive but
\begin{align}
    \label{eq:app-ising-slow} \tau_{\operatorname{mix}}^{\mathcal{L}_1+\mathcal{L}_2}(1/4) \geq e^{c_\beta L}=e^{c_\beta\sqrt N}
\end{align}
for some $c_\beta>0$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end example-8 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
\renewcommand{\getrefnumber{#1}}{\getrefnumber{app:ex:ising-kernel-mismatch}} 
  \refstepcounter{proof} 
  \label{proof:ising-kernel-mismatch} 

Let $C_1,C_2$ be the two checkerboard colors. For each site $x$, let $T_x$ be the conditional heat-bath reset: measure its neighbors in the $Z$ basis and replace spin $x$ by its conditional Gibbs state, acting as the identity elsewhere. Write $\partial x$ for the neighbors of $x$ and $\eta\in\{\pm1\}^{\partial x}$ for their spin configuration, with projector $\Pi_\eta:=\bigotimes_{y\in\partial x}\frac{\mathbb{I}_y+\eta_yZ_y}{2}$. In the basis $Z|s\rangle=s|s\rangle$, the operator form is
\begin{align}
    p_x(s\mid\eta)&:=\frac{e^{\beta s\sum_{y\in\partial x}\eta_y}}{2\cosh\!\left(\beta\sum_{y\in\partial x}\eta_y\right)},\qquad s\in\{\pm1\},\notag\\
    J_{x,\eta,s,u}&:=\sqrt{p_x(s\mid\eta)}\,|s\rangle\langle u|_x\otimes\Pi_\eta,\qquad s,u\in\{\pm1\},\notag\\
    T_x(\rho)&:=\sum_{\eta\in\{\pm1\}^{\partial x}}\sum_{s,u\in\{\pm1\}}J_{x,\eta,s,u}\rho J_{x,\eta,s,u}^\dagger, \label{eq:ising-conditional-reset}
\end{align}
where each $J_{x,\eta,s,u}$ is tensored with the identity outside $\{x\}\cup\partial x$. Set
\begin{align}
    \mathcal{L}_i&:=\sum_{x\in C_i}(T_x-\operatorname{id}),\qquad E_i:=\prod_{x\in C_i}T_x. \label{eq:ising-layer-construction}
\end{align}
These are geometrically 5-local, purely dissipative generators. Since $\sigma_{\beta,L}$ is diagonal, measuring the neighbors leaves it unchanged; resampling spin $x$ from its conditional Gibbs distribution also preserves it. Thus $T_x(\sigma_{\beta,L})=\sigma_{\beta,L}$ for every $x$, and $\mathcal{L}_i(\sigma_{\beta,L})=0$ for $i=1,2$. The resets are idempotent and commute within each color. The standard conditional-reset MLSI gives $\alpha(T_x-\operatorname{id})\geq1/2$ \cite[Example~3.2]{Bardet2017}, and \cref{prop:mlsi-commuting} therefore gives $\alpha(\mathcal{L}_i)\geq1/2$.

We now derive the mixing estimate in \cref{eq:app-ising-layer-rm}. For $x\in C_i$, idempotence gives
\begin{align}
    S_x(t):=e^{t(T_x-\operatorname{id})}
    =T_x+e^{-t}(\operatorname{id}-T_x).
\end{align}
Because the resets commute within one color, if $C_i=\{x_1,\ldots,x_m\}$ then
\begin{align}
    e^{t\mathcal{L}_i}=\prod_{k=1}^m S_{x_k}(t),
    \qquad
    P_{\mathcal{L}_i}=E_i=\prod_{k=1}^m T_{x_k}.
\end{align}
The difference of these products has the telescoping expansion
\begin{align}
    e^{t\mathcal{L}_i}-E_i
    =\sum_{k=1}^m
    \left(\prod_{j<k}S_{x_j}(t)\right)
    \bigl(S_{x_k}(t)-T_{x_k}\bigr)
    \left(\prod_{j>k}T_{x_j}\right).
\end{align}
Every $S_x(t)$ and $T_x$ is a quantum channel and therefore has diamond norm one. Moreover,
$S_x(t)-T_x=e^{-t}(\operatorname{id}-T_x)$ and
$\|\operatorname{id}-T_x\|_\diamond\leq2$. Hence submultiplicativity and the triangle inequality give
\begin{align}
    \|e^{t\mathcal{L}_i}-P_{\mathcal{L}_i}\|_\diamond
    &\leq\sum_{k=1}^m e^{-t}\|\operatorname{id}-T_{x_k}\|_\diamond
    \leq2|C_i|e^{-t}\leq2Ne^{-t}.
\end{align}
Applying this channel bound to any state $\rho$ gives \cref{eq:app-ising-layer-rm}.

The map $P_{\mathcal{L}_i}=E_i$ preserves an arbitrary diagonal marginal on the opposite color and puts $C_i$ in its conditional Gibbs state. Thus the two fixed-point spaces are different and nontrivial.

We use the criterion in \cite{Frigerio1978}: a finite-dimensional Lindbladian with a full-rank stationary state is primitive if the only operators commuting with its Hamiltonian, all jumps, and their adjoints are scalar multiples of the identity. Here the Hamiltonian vanishes, and $p_x(s\mid\eta)>0$ for every spin configuration. The jumps in \cref{eq:ising-conditional-reset} satisfy
\begin{align*}
    \sum_\eta p_x(s\mid\eta)^{-1/2}J_{x,\eta,s,u}
    =|s\rangle\langle u|_x\otimes\mathbb{I}_{x^c}.
\end{align*}
Thus an operator commuting with every jump commutes with every single-site matrix unit, and must be a scalar multiple of $\mathbb{I}$. Since $\sigma_{\beta,L}$ is full rank, the sum $\mathcal{L}_1+\mathcal{L}_2$ is primitive. The intersection of the fixed-point spaces is the span of $\sigma_{\beta,L}$.
The low-temperature mixing-time lower bound in \cref{eq:app-ising-slow} follows from \cite[Corollary~3.5 and Lemma~4.14]{GKZ2024} for the two-dimensional Ising model.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- example-9: body_md -->
\label{app:ex:rm_sum_dissip_only}
Consider a periodic chain of $N\geq2$ sites, with two qubits $a_i,b_i$ at each site $i$. Define the families $(\mathcal{L}_N)_N$ and $(\mathcal{K}_N)_N$ by writing $\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_N$ and $\mathcal{K}=\mathcal{K}_N$ at each size:
\begin{align}
    \mathcal{L}&=\sum_{i=1}^N\mathcal{D}[L_{a,i}]+\sum_{i=1}^N\mathcal{D}[L_{b,i}]+\sum_{i=1}^N\mathcal{D}[L_{a,b,i}],\notag\\
    \mathcal{K}&=\sum_{i=1}^N\mathcal{D}[K_{a,i}]+\sum_{i=1}^N\mathcal{D}[L_{b,i}]+\sum_{i=1}^N\mathcal{D}[L_{a,b,i}],\label{rows-eq:two-dissipators}
\end{align}
with jump operators
\begin{align}
    L_{a,i}&=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\
    0&-1\end{pmatrix}_{a_i},\qquad 1\le i\le N,\notag\\
    K_{a,i}&=\begin{pmatrix}1&-2\\
    0&-1\end{pmatrix}_{a_i},\qquad 1\le i\le N,\notag\\
    L_{b,i}&=\lvert 0\rangle\!\langle 0\rvert_{b_i}\otimes\lvert 0\rangle\!\langle 1\rvert_{b_{i+1}},\qquad 1\le i\le N,\notag\\
    L_{a,b,i}&=\sqrt{\gamma}\,\lvert 1\rangle\!\langle 1\rvert_{a_i}\otimes\lvert 0\rangle\!\langle 1\rvert_{b_i},\qquad 1\le i\le N.\label{rows-eq:two-dissipator-jumps}
\end{align}
Here $\gamma>0$ is independent of $N$, and the site labels are understood modulo $N$, so $b_{N+1}=b_1$. The bottom jump changes $b_{i+1}$ from $1$ to $0$ when $b_i$ is in state $0$, while the cross jump changes $b_i$ from $1$ to $0$ when $a_i$ is in state $1$. Thus $\mathcal{L}$ and $\mathcal{K}$ are translation invariant and have the same bottom and cross jumps, while the off-diagonal entries of their $a_i$ jumps have opposite signs.

Let $\eta=\begin{pmatrix}\frac56&-\frac13\\-\frac13&\frac16\end{pmatrix}$ be the unique fixed point of the single-qubit dissipator with jump operator $L_a=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$. The Lindbladian $\mathcal{L}$ has the unique fixed point $\sigma_\mathcal{L}=\eta_a^{\otimes N}\otimes\lvert 0^N\rangle\!\langle 0^N\rvert_b$, while $\mathcal{K}$ has the unique fixed point $\sigma_\mathcal{K}=(Z\eta Z)_a^{\otimes N}\otimes\lvert 0^N\rangle\!\langle 0^N\rvert_b$. Both families $(\mathcal{L}_N)_N$ and $(\mathcal{K}_N)_N$ are dissipation-only and rapidly mixing with constant decay rate, but $(\mathcal{L}_N+\mathcal{K}_N)_N$ is not rapidly mixing: for every fixed $0<\delta<1/2$, $\tau_{\operatorname{mix}}^{\mathcal{L}+\mathcal{K}}(\delta)=\Omega(N)$.

Their sum has kernel
\begin{align}
    \ker(\mathcal{L}+\mathcal{K})&=\lvert 0^N\rangle\!\langle 0^N\rvert_a\otimes\mathcal{B}(\mathcal S_b),\qquad \mathcal S_b:=\operatorname{span}\{|0^N\rangle_b,|1^N\rangle_b\},
\end{align}
where $\mathcal{B}(\mathcal S_b)$ is embedded in the $b$-qubit operator algebra and includes coherences between the strings. Its infinite-time limit exists, and the mixing time to this kernel is $\Omega(N)$.
<!-- end example-9 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
\renewcommand{\getrefnumber{#1}}{\getrefnumber{lem:rm_sum_dissip_only}} 
  \refstepcounter{proof} 
  \label{proof:rm_sum_dissip_only} 

\emph{Rapid mixing of each summand.} We prove rapid mixing for $\mathcal{L}$ with the following strategy. First we bound how quickly the $b$ qubits approach $\lvert 0^N\rangle\!\langle 0^N\rvert_b$. At the intermediate time $s:=t/2$, we then replace the evolved state $\rho_s:=e^{s\mathcal{L}}(\rho)$ by a nearby state $\zeta=\zeta_a\otimes\lvert 0^N\rangle\!\langle 0^N\rvert_b$ whose $b$ qubits have reached the steady state. Finally, on this exact $b$-vacuum, the bottom and cross terms vanish and the $a$ qubits evolve as the tensor product $T_s^{\otimes N}$ of the one-qubit semigroup $T_s:=e^{s\mathcal{D}[L_a]}$. The bounds proved below give
\begin{align}
    \|e^{t\mathcal{L}}(\rho)-\sigma_\mathcal{L}\|_1&\overset{(1)}{\le}\|\rho_s-\zeta\|_1+\|T_s^{\otimes N}(\zeta_a)-\eta_a^{\otimes N}\|_1,\notag\\
    &\overset{(2)}{\le}2\sqrt{8N}\,e^{-\lambda t}+CNe^{-ct/2},\notag\\
    &\overset{(3)}{\le}(2\sqrt8+C)Ne^{-at},\qquad a:=\min\{\lambda,c/2\},\label{rows-eq:upper}
\end{align}
where $(1)$ uses the triangle inequality proved in \cref{rows-eq:two-stage-triangle}, $(2)$ uses the $b$-qubit replacement bound \cref{rows-eq:projection-applied} and the $a$-qubit tensor-product bound \cref{rows-eq:top-product}, and $(3)$ uses $\sqrt N\le N$ and the definition of $a$. This is rapid mixing with constant decay rate. We now prove each of these bounds.

It is enough to prove this estimate for times satisfying $8Ne^{-2\lambda t}<1$. Indeed, for the complementary times the trivial estimate $\|e^{t\mathcal{L}}(\rho)-\sigma_\mathcal{L}\|_1\le2$ can be absorbed into the prefactor in \cref{rows-eq:upper}. This restriction will ensure that the normalized projection used below is well defined.

We first study how quickly the $b$ qubits approach $\lvert 0^N\rangle\!\langle 0^N\rvert_b$. Let $n_{b_j}:=\lvert 1\rangle\!\langle 1\rvert_{b_j}$ and $\rho_t:=e^{t\mathcal{L}}(\rho)$. Our goal is to bound the decay of $\operatorname{Tr}(n_{b_j}\rho_t)$, the probability that qubit $b_j$ is occupied. It suffices to find a positive one-qubit matrix $h$ and a constant $\lambda>0$ such that the observable $h_{a_j}n_{b_j}$ on the pair $a_j,b_j$ satisfies
\begin{align}
    \mathcal{L}^*(h_{a_j}n_{b_j})&\preceq-4\lambda h_{a_j}n_{b_j},\label{rows-eq:required-adjoint}\\
    \tfrac14 n_{b_j}&\preceq h_{a_j}n_{b_j}\preceq2n_{b_j}.\label{rows-eq:occupation-comparison}
\end{align}
The first inequality controls its decay; the second compares it with the occupation. If these inequalities hold, then
\begin{align}
    \frac{d}{dt}\operatorname{Tr}(h_{a_j}n_{b_j}\rho_t)&\overset{(1)}{\le}-4\lambda\operatorname{Tr}(h_{a_j}n_{b_j}\rho_t),\notag\\
    \operatorname{Tr}(h_{a_j}n_{b_j}\rho_t)&\overset{(2)}{\le}e^{-4\lambda t}\operatorname{Tr}(h_{a_j}n_{b_j}\rho),\label{rows-eq:weighted-decay}
\end{align}
where $(1)$ follows by taking the expectation of \cref{rows-eq:required-adjoint} in $\rho_t$, and $(2)$ follows by integration. Using this decay estimate, we obtain
\begin{align}
    \operatorname{Tr}(n_{b_j}\rho_t)&\overset{(1)}{\le}4\operatorname{Tr}(h_{a_j}n_{b_j}\rho_t),\notag\\
    &\overset{(2)}{\le}4e^{-4\lambda t}\operatorname{Tr}(h_{a_j}n_{b_j}\rho),\notag\\
    &\overset{(3)}{\le}8e^{-4\lambda t},\label{rows-eq:site-bound}
\end{align}
where $(1)$ uses the lower bound in \cref{rows-eq:occupation-comparison}, $(2)$ uses \cref{rows-eq:weighted-decay}, and $(3)$ uses the upper bound in \cref{rows-eq:occupation-comparison} together with $\operatorname{Tr}(n_{b_j}\rho)\le1$. We now construct $h$ and prove \cref{rows-eq:required-adjoint} and \cref{rows-eq:occupation-comparison}.

To obtain \cref{rows-eq:required-adjoint}, we look for a real symmetric matrix $h$ with $h_{00}=1$. On $h_{a_j}n_{b_j}$, the top jump contributes $\mathcal{D}[L_a]^*(h)_{a_j}n_{b_j}$, where $L_a=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&2\\0&-1\end{smallmatrix}\right)$. The cross jump contributes $-\gamma\{\lvert 1\rangle\!\langle 1\rvert,h\}_{a_j}n_{b_j}/2$: its jump term vanishes because $\lvert 1\rangle\!\langle 0\rvert\lvert 1\rangle\!\langle 1\rvert\lvert 0\rangle\!\langle 1\rvert=0$. The incoming bottom edge removes the occupation at $b_j$ when $b_{j-1}$ is empty, while the outgoing edge and its adjoint commute with $h_{a_j}n_{b_j}$. All other jumps have disjoint support. Therefore
\begin{align}
    \mathcal{L}^*(h_{a_j}n_{b_j})&=\bigl(\mathcal{D}[L_a]^*(h)-\tfrac\gamma2\{\lvert 1\rangle\!\langle 1\rvert,h\}\bigr)_{a_j}n_{b_j}
    -h_{a_j}\lvert 0\rangle\!\langle 0\rvert_{b_{j-1}}n_{b_j},\label{rows-eq:pair-action}
\end{align}
where $j-1$ is understood modulo $N$.
For $h=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&h_{01}\\h_{01}&h_{11}\end{smallmatrix}\right)$, direct multiplication gives
\begin{align}
    \mathcal{D}[L_a]^*(h)-\tfrac\gamma2\{\lvert 1\rangle\!\langle 1\rvert,h\}&=\begin{pmatrix}-2h_{01}&1-h_{11}-(4+\gamma/2)h_{01}\\
    1-h_{11}-(4+\gamma/2)h_{01}&4-6h_{01}-(4+\gamma)h_{11}\end{pmatrix}.\label{rows-eq:drift-matrix}
\end{align}
We make this matrix diagonal and negative. First impose $4-(4+\gamma)h_{11}=-\gamma/2$, so its lower-right entry becomes $-\gamma/2-6h_{01}$. Then cancel its off-diagonal entries. Solving these two equations in order gives
\begin{align}
    h_{11}&=\frac{4+\gamma/2}{4+\gamma}=\frac{\gamma+8}{2(\gamma+4)},\qquad h_{01}=\frac{1-h_{11}}{4+\gamma/2}=\frac{\gamma}{(\gamma+4)(\gamma+8)}>0.\notag
\end{align}
Thus both diagonal entries in \cref{rows-eq:drift-matrix} are negative. We have obtained
\begin{align}
    h&=\begin{pmatrix}1&\dfrac{\gamma}{(\gamma+4)(\gamma+8)}\\
    \dfrac{\gamma}{(\gamma+4)(\gamma+8)}&\dfrac{\gamma+8}{2(\gamma+4)}\end{pmatrix},\qquad \lambda:=\frac{h_{01}}4=\frac{\gamma}{4(\gamma+4)(\gamma+8)}.\notag
\end{align}
Here $1/2\le h_{11}\le1$ and $0<h_{01}\le1/8$. Bounding the cross term of its quadratic form by $2|u_0u_1|\le|u_0|^2+|u_1|^2$ gives $\frac38\mathbb{I}\preceq h\preceq\frac98\mathbb{I}$. In particular, $h$ is positive and $h\preceq2\mathbb{I}$; also $0<\lambda\le1/32$. Substituting the chosen entries into \cref{rows-eq:drift-matrix} therefore yields
\begin{align}
    \mathcal{D}[L_a]^*(h)-\tfrac\gamma2\{\lvert 1\rangle\!\langle 1\rvert,h\}&=\operatorname{diag}(-8\lambda,-\gamma/2-24\lambda)\preceq-8\lambda\mathbb{I}\preceq-4\lambda h.\label{rows-eq:killed}
\end{align}
The last term of \cref{rows-eq:pair-action} is negative semidefinite because it is a tensor product of positive factors with a minus sign. Hence $\mathcal{L}^*(h_{a_j}n_{b_j})\preceq-4\lambda h_{a_j}n_{b_j}$, proving \cref{rows-eq:required-adjoint}.

For \cref{rows-eq:occupation-comparison}, the bounds on $h$ give $\frac14\mathbb{I}\preceq h\preceq2\mathbb{I}$. Since $h_{a_j}$ and $n_{b_j}$ act on different qubits, tensoring with the positive projector $n_{b_j}$ gives $\frac14 n_{b_j}\preceq h_{a_j}n_{b_j}\preceq2n_{b_j}$. Both required inequalities are therefore established, so \cref{rows-eq:site-bound} holds for every initial state.

With $P:=\mathbb{I}_a\otimes \lvert 0^N\rangle\!\langle 0^N\rvert_b$, the quantity $p_t:=\operatorname{Tr}((\mathbb{I}-P)\rho_t)$ is the probability that at least one $b$ qubit is occupied. The indicator of this event is bounded by the number of occupied sites, so $\mathbb{I}-P\preceq\sum_jn_{b_j}$. Summing the preceding estimate with \cref{rows-eq:site-bound} gives
\begin{align}
    p_t&\le\sum_{j=1}^N\operatorname{Tr}(n_{b_j}\rho_t)\le8N e^{-4\lambda t}.\label{rows-eq:clearing}
\end{align}
\cref{rows-eq:clearing} controls the weight outside the $b$-vacuum $\lvert 0^N\rangle\!\langle 0^N\rvert_b$. We now study how large $t$ needs to be so that projecting to a state with the $b$ qubits exactly in $\lvert 0^N\rangle\!\langle 0^N\rvert_b$ is a good enough approximation for rapid mixing. Set $s:=t/2$ and $\rho_s:=e^{s\mathcal{L}}(\rho)$. We will construct a state $\zeta$ supported on $P$ and close to $\rho_s$, of the form $\zeta=\zeta_a\otimes\lvert 0^N\rangle\!\langle 0^N\rvert_b$. If we find such a $\zeta$, all bottom and cross jumps vanish on the $b$-vacuum, so only the top jumps remain and the $a$ qubits evolve independently. Thus, writing $T_u:=e^{u\mathcal{D}[L_a]}$, we have $e^{s\mathcal{L}}(\zeta)=T_s^{\otimes N}(\zeta_a)\otimes\lvert 0^N\rangle\!\langle 0^N\rvert_b$. The triangle inequality and contraction of the trace norm under $e^{s\mathcal{L}}$ therefore give
\begin{align}
    \|e^{t\mathcal{L}}(\rho)-\sigma_\mathcal{L}\|_1&=\|e^{s\mathcal{L}}(\rho_s)-\sigma_\mathcal{L}\|_1,\notag\\
    &\overset{(1)}{\le}\|e^{s\mathcal{L}}(\rho_s)-e^{s\mathcal{L}}(\zeta)\|_1+\|e^{s\mathcal{L}}(\zeta)-\sigma_\mathcal{L}\|_1,\notag\\
    &\overset{(2)}{\le}\|\rho_s-\zeta\|_1+\|\bigl(T_s^{\otimes N}(\zeta_a)-\eta_a^{\otimes N}\bigr)\otimes\lvert 0^N\rangle\!\langle 0^N\rvert_b\|_1,\notag\\
    &\overset{(3)}{=}\|\rho_s-\zeta\|_1+\|T_s^{\otimes N}(\zeta_a)-\eta_a^{\otimes N}\|_1,\label{rows-eq:two-stage-triangle}
\end{align}
where $(1)$ is the triangle inequality, $(2)$ uses contractivity for the first term and the expressions for $e^{s\mathcal{L}}(\zeta)$ and $\sigma_\mathcal{L}$, and $(3)$ uses multiplicativity of the trace norm together with $\|\lvert 0^N\rangle\!\langle 0^N\rvert_b\|_1=1$. Thus the first term in \cref{rows-eq:two-stage-triangle} is the error from replacing the $b$ qubits by the exact vacuum, while the second is the remaining $a$-qubit mixing error. We now construct $\zeta$ and bound these two terms.

For the first term, we use the following normalized-projector form of the gentle-measurement lemma \cite[Lemma~9]{winter1999coding}. For any state $\xi$, let $p:=\operatorname{Tr}((\mathbb{I}-P)\xi)$ and, when $p<1$, let $\zeta:=P\xi P/(1-p)$. Then
\begin{align}
    \|\xi-\zeta\|_1&\le2\sqrt p.\label{rows-eq:projection}
\end{align}
For completeness, we give the short purification proof. Let $\lvert\Psi\rangle$ be a purification of $\xi$ on the system and a reference space, so $\operatorname{Tr}_{\mathrm{ref}}\lvert \Psi\rangle\!\langle \Psi\rvert=\xi$, and put $q:=\operatorname{Tr}(P\xi)=1-p$. First,
\begin{align}
    \|(P\otimes\mathbb{I})\lvert\Psi\rangle\|^2&\overset{(1)}{=}\langle\Psi\vert(P\otimes\mathbb{I})^2\vert\Psi\rangle,\notag\\
    &\overset{(2)}{=}\langle\Psi\vert(P\otimes\mathbb{I})\vert\Psi\rangle,\notag\\
    &\overset{(3)}{=}\operatorname{Tr}\!\left((P\otimes\mathbb{I})\lvert \Psi\rangle\!\langle \Psi\rvert\right)=\operatorname{Tr}(P\xi)=q,\label{rows-eq:projected-norm}
\end{align}
where $(1)$ is the definition of the squared norm, $(2)$ uses $P^2=P$, and $(3)$ uses the defining partial-trace identity for the purification. Hence, when $q>0$, the projected vector
\begin{align}
    \lvert\Phi\rangle&:=\frac{(P\otimes\mathbb{I})\lvert\Psi\rangle}{\sqrt q}.\notag
\end{align}
is normalized. It is a purification of $\zeta$ because
\begin{align}
    \operatorname{Tr}_{\mathrm{ref}}\lvert \Phi\rangle\!\langle \Phi\rvert&\overset{(1)}{=}\frac{P\bigl(\operatorname{Tr}_{\mathrm{ref}}\lvert \Psi\rangle\!\langle \Psi\rvert\bigr)P}{q},\notag\\
    &\overset{(2)}{=}\frac{P\xi P}{q}=\zeta,
\end{align}
where $(1)$ substitutes the definition of $\lvert\Phi\rangle$ and pulls the system operators through the partial trace, while $(2)$ uses $\operatorname{Tr}_{\mathrm{ref}}\lvert \Psi\rangle\!\langle \Psi\rvert=\xi$. Its overlap with the original purification is
\begin{align}
    \langle\Psi\vert\Phi\rangle&\overset{(1)}{=}\frac{\langle\Psi\vert(P\otimes\mathbb{I})\vert\Psi\rangle}{\sqrt q},\notag\\
    &\overset{(2)}{=}\frac{\operatorname{Tr}(P\xi)}{\sqrt q},\notag\\
    &\overset{(3)}{=}\frac{q}{\sqrt q}=\sqrt q=\sqrt{1-p},\label{rows-eq:purification-overlap}
\end{align}
where $(1)$ uses the definition of $\lvert\Phi\rangle$, $(2)$ uses the partial-trace identity, and $(3)$ uses $q=\operatorname{Tr}(P\xi)=1-p$. In particular, there is no hidden phase: $\langle\Psi\vert(P\otimes\mathbb{I})\vert\Psi\rangle$ is the expectation of a positive projector, so it is the real nonnegative number $q$. Contractivity under the partial trace and the pure-state trace-distance formula now give
\begin{align}
    \|\xi-\zeta\|_1&\overset{(1)}{\le}\|\lvert \Psi\rangle\!\langle \Psi\rvert-\lvert \Phi\rangle\!\langle \Phi\rvert\|_1,\notag\\
    &\overset{(2)}{=}2\sqrt{1-|\langle\Psi\vert\Phi\rangle|^2},\notag\\
    &\overset{(3)}{=}2\sqrt p,
\end{align}
where $(1)$ uses contractivity of the partial trace, $(2)$ is the trace distance between two pure states, and $(3)$ uses \cref{rows-eq:purification-overlap}. This proves \cref{rows-eq:projection} and is exactly where positivity of $\xi$ controls the coherences between the vacuum and nonvacuum sectors. In the time regime fixed above, \cref{rows-eq:clearing} gives $p_s\le8Ne^{-4\lambda s}=8Ne^{-2\lambda t}<1$, so the normalized projected state is well defined. Applying the estimate to $\xi=\rho_s$ gives
\begin{align}
    \|\rho_s-\zeta\|_1&\overset{(1)}{\le}2\sqrt{p_s},\notag\\
    &\overset{(2)}{\le}2\sqrt{8N}\,e^{-2\lambda s},\notag\\
    &\overset{(3)}{=}2\sqrt{8N}\,e^{-\lambda t},\label{rows-eq:projection-applied}
\end{align}
where $(1)$ uses \cref{rows-eq:projection}, $(2)$ uses \cref{rows-eq:clearing} at time $s$, and $(3)$ uses $s=t/2$.

It remains to bound the second term in \cref{rows-eq:two-stage-triangle}. The one-qubit semigroup $T_t$ is primitive with stationary state $\eta$: indeed, $\eta$ is positive with trace $1$, direct substitution gives $\mathcal{D}[L_a](\eta)=0$, and direct diagonalization shows that the eigenvalue $0$ of $\mathcal{D}[L_a]$ is simple, while its nonzero eigenvalues are $-2,-4,-6$. Since this is a fixed finite-dimensional semigroup, there are constants $C,c>0$, independent of $N$, such that its asymptotic channel $E_a(B):=\eta\operatorname{Tr} B$ satisfies
\begin{align}
    \|T_t-E_a\|_\diamond&\le Ce^{-ct}.\label{row:Tt-Etop}
\end{align}
We may therefore telescope directly in diamond norm:
\begin{align}
    T_t^{\otimes N}-E_a^{\otimes N}&=\sum_{j=1}^NE_a^{\otimes(j-1)}\otimes(T_t-E_a)\otimes T_t^{\otimes(N-j)}.
\end{align}
Both $T_t$ and $E_a$ are channels and hence have diamond norm $1$. The triangle inequality and multiplicativity of the diamond norm thus give
\begin{align}
    \|T_t^{\otimes N}(\zeta_a)-\eta_a^{\otimes N}\|_1&\overset{(1)}{\le}\|T_t^{\otimes N}-E_a^{\otimes N}\|_\diamond,\notag\\
    &\overset{(2)}{\le}\sum_{j=1}^N\|T_t-E_a\|_\diamond,\notag\\
    &\overset{(3)}{\le}CNe^{-ct},\label{rows-eq:top-product}
\end{align}
for every $a$-qubit state $\zeta_a$, where $(1)$ uses $E_a^{\otimes N}(\zeta_a)=\eta_a^{\otimes N}$ and the definition of the diamond norm, $(2)$ uses the triangle inequality applied to the telescoping identity together with $\|T_t\|_\diamond=\|E_a\|_\diamond=1$, and $(3)$ uses \cref{row:Tt-Etop}.

Together, \cref{rows-eq:projection-applied,rows-eq:top-product} establish the second step of \cref{rows-eq:upper}, and hence prove the stated constant-decay-rate rapid-mixing estimate for $\mathcal{L}$.

It remains to verify stationarity and transfer the bound to $\mathcal{K}$. The stationary $a$-qubit state and the $b$-vacuum restriction show that $\mathcal{L}(\sigma_\mathcal{L})=0$, and convergence in \cref{rows-eq:upper} proves uniqueness. Put $U:=Z_a^{\otimes N}\otimes\mathbb{I}_b$ and $\mathcal U(B):=UBU^\dagger$. We have $\mathcal{K}=\mathcal U\mathcal{L}\mathcal U^{-1}$ because $ZL_aZ=K_a$ and $Z\lvert 1\rangle\!\langle 1\rvert Z=\lvert 1\rangle\!\langle 1\rvert$, while $U$ acts trivially on the $b$ qubits. Its unique stationary state is therefore $\sigma_\mathcal{K}=\mathcal U(\sigma_\mathcal{L})$, and unitary invariance of trace norm gives the same bound \cref{rows-eq:upper} for $\mathcal{K}$. Thus both generators are rapidly mixing with the same constant decay rate.

\emph{Stationary space and infinite-time limit of the sum.} Write $s_i=\lvert 0\rangle\!\langle 1\rvert_{a_i}$, $n_i^a=\lvert 1\rangle\!\langle 1\rvert_{a_i}$, and $n_i^b=\lvert 1\rangle\!\langle 1\rvert_{b_i}$. Expanding the two top dissipators gives
\begin{align}
    \mathcal D[Z+2s]+\mathcal D[Z-2s]&=2\mathcal D[Z]+8\mathcal D[s],\notag\\
    (\mathcal{L}+\mathcal{K})^*(n_i^a)&=-8n_i^a.
\end{align}
Thus every stationary state has zero $a$-qubit occupation and, by positivity, is supported on the $a$-vacuum. On this sector the cross dissipators vanish. The total $b$-qubit occupation then satisfies
\begin{align}
    (\mathcal{L}+\mathcal{K})^*\left(\sum_{i=1}^N n_i^b\right) &=-2\sum_{i=1}^{N}(\mathbb{I}-n_i^b)n_{i+1}^b,
\end{align}
where this identity is restricted to the $a$-vacuum sector and $n_{N+1}^b=n_1^b$. Each summand on the right is a positive projector onto a cyclic neighboring $01$ pattern. A stationary state must therefore be supported on cyclic strings without $01$. Any nonconstant cyclic binary string contains both a transition from $0$ to $1$ and a transition from $1$ to $0$, so the only such strings are $|0^N\rangle_b$ and $|1^N\rangle_b$, precisely the strings spanning $\mathcal S_b$. Conversely, each bottom jump annihilates $\mathcal S_b$, so both its jump term and its anticommutator vanish on every operator in $\mathcal{B}(\mathcal S_b)$.

To establish convergence on all operators, order the computational matrix units $|x\rangle\langle y|$ by the total number of ones in $x$ and $y$. Each lowering jump lowers this number when its jump term is nonzero; the anticommutator terms and the $a$-qubit $Z$ dissipators are diagonal in this basis. The generator is therefore triangular with real nonpositive diagonal. Its zero diagonal entries are exactly the matrix units supported on the $a$-vacuum and $\mathcal S_b$ in both ket and bra. The semigroup is bounded in induced trace norm, so zero has no nontrivial Jordan block: such a block would produce polynomial growth on its generalized eigenspace. All other eigenvalues are strictly negative. This proves the asserted kernel, and $P_{\mathcal{L}+\mathcal{K}}$ exists by \cref{lem:infinite-time-limit}.

\emph{Mixing-time lower bound for the sum.} We prove the lower bound on the mixing time of $\mathcal{L}+\mathcal{K}$ by finding an initial state that takes $\Omega(N)$ time to mix. For $0\le j\le N-1$, write $\lvert d_j\rangle_b:=\lvert0^{N-j}1^j\rangle_b$ and define
\begin{align}
    \omega_j&:=\lvert 0^N\rangle\!\langle 0^N\rvert_a\otimes\lvert d_j\rangle\!\langle d_j\rvert_b.
\end{align}
We take $\rho_{\mathrm{in}}:=\omega_{N-1}$. Since $L_a=Z+2\lvert 0\rangle\!\langle 1\rvert$ and $K_a=Z-2\lvert 0\rangle\!\langle 1\rvert$, the mixed terms in their dissipators cancel, and the remaining top dissipators vanish on $\lvert 0\rangle\!\langle 0\rvert$. Every cross jump contains the $a$-qubit projector $\lvert 1\rangle\!\langle 1\rvert$, which annihilates $\lvert0\rangle$, so both the jump and anticommutator terms of its dissipator vanish on the $a$-vacuum. Finally, for $1\leq j\leq N-1$, the cyclic string $d_j=0^{N-j}1^j$ has a unique neighboring pattern $01$, at sites $(N-j,N-j+1)$; the wraparound pair is $10$. Thus only $L_{b,N-j}$ acts. Since each bottom dissipator appears once in $\mathcal{L}$ and once in $\mathcal{K}$, we obtain
\begin{align}
    (\mathcal{L}+\mathcal{K})(\omega_j)&=2(\omega_{j-1}-\omega_j)\qquad(1\le j\le N-1),\notag\\
    (\mathcal{L}+\mathcal{K})(\omega_0)&=0.\label{rows-eq:dissip-omega-action}
\end{align}
Thus the span of the $\omega_j$ is invariant and the evolution on it is classical. In particular,
\begin{align}
    e^{t(\mathcal{L}+\mathcal{K})}(\rho_{\mathrm{in}})&=\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}q_j(t)\omega_j,
\end{align}
where $q_{N-1}(0)=1$, $q_j(0)=0$ for $j<N-1$, and the coefficients satisfy the system of differential equations
\begin{align}
    q_{N-1}'(t)&=-2q_{N-1}(t),\notag\\
    q_j'(t)&=2q_{j+1}(t)-2q_j(t)\qquad(1\le j<N-1),\notag\\
    q_0'(t)&=2q_1(t).\label{rows-eq:bottom-ode}
\end{align}
The first equation gives $q_{N-1}(t)\to0$, and the middle equations then give $q_j(t)\to0$ successively for every $j\ge1$. Since $\sum_jq_j(t)=1$, we have $q_0(t)\to1$. Thus this trajectory converges to $\sigma_{\mathcal{L}+\mathcal{K}}:=\omega_0$, and the existence of $P_{\mathcal{L}+\mathcal{K}}$ just proved implies $P_{\mathcal{L}+\mathcal{K}}(\rho_{\mathrm{in}})=\sigma_{\mathcal{L}+\mathcal{K}}=\omega_0$.
